speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house may be interested if I make a brief report on a meeting which was held in my office this morning of the leaders of four parties. There was one party leader missing, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), and he had indicated previously that he would not be at the meeting this morning.
Mr. Speaker, we met this morning, I think I can say for us all, very conscious of our responsibilities and very anxious to reach agreement on a way out of what I think I can call a parliamentary impasse on the flag debate, an agreement which could be conducive to a decision being reached without long delay on this matter, and with a maximum of agreement. To adapt the analogy of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, at the very friendly meeting this morning there were no bulls and no toreadors. There were not even any picadors.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext:
Like all the best witticisms, Mr. Speaker, that one was entirely unintended.
At the meeting we discussed, as I said, a way out of our difficulty. As the house knows, agreement in principle was reached some time ago about the reference of this question to a committee; the difficulty was in reaching agreement on how the committee would operate and what would happen when its report was submitted to the house. These difficulties, Mr. Speaker, were cleared off this morning when we agreed on the following procedure.
The current flag debate should be suspended and the matter referred to a committee by a resolution which in agreed terms should be put on the order paper as soon as possible. The house leader would be willing, indeed anxious, to consult house leaders of the other
parties later this afternoon on the terms of a resolution of this kind, and if agreement could be reached on those terms this afternoon and if the house were willing to give unanimous agreement later in the day, then that resolution could be disposed of by unanimous agreement with a minimum of delay and the committee could be set up and put to work at once.
The committee, as we agreed this morning, will consist of 15 members; 7 Liberals, 5 Conservatives, 1 New Democrat, 1 Social Crediter and 1 Creditiste. It was agreed that the committee would report back to the house in the normal way within six weeks.
The committee will meet-and I should emphasize this-after there has already been an exhaustive consideration of all sides of the question in the house. Perhaps it should also be pointed out that this consideration was given by the house during the time when normally there would have been a parliamentary recess. While the committee would, of course, determine its own procedure, we felt-and I think I can speak for the other leaders on this point-that there would be a better chance of reaching an agreed solution, and that is our objective, if those meetings or at least most of them could be confidential. I think that would be conducive to the most constructive kind of consideration and discussion.
When the committee's report was ready there would be another meeting of the party leaders to determine the length of time that should be devoted in the house to a discussion of that report. If the report were unanimous or virtually unanimous, as I sincerely hope it will be, then there would be no problem because the subsequent debate would, I am sure, be a very short one. If there were a strong division of opinion in the committee and a substantial and strongly held minority view, then of course there would be a problem.
So far as the government are concerned, and having regard to the long debate we have already had, we maintain both the view that a reasonable time limit would then be essential and also the hope that it could be obtained by agreement. However, Mr. Speaker, a decision on this matter is to be

Canadian Flag
deferred and perhaps, as 1 have said, the work of the committee will make that decision not a difficult one.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, the proposed committee will be successful in its work. It begins that work, I know, with the good will of all members on all sides of the house. We have had our strong differences of opinion on this flag issue. They have been sincerely held and vigorously expressed, and this is not the first time in Canadian history that differences have been strongly held and vigorously expressed over a considerable period of time. While we may have these differences, and while we may express these differences very strongly, I know, Mr. Speaker, we have no differences in our devotion and loyalty to a strong and united Canada.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext: If we are honest in our differences, as I believe we are, we have only one thought in the discussion of these differences; the unity of our country, pride in its progress and faith in its destiny.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister spoke well and effectively when he stated that strong differences of opinion make for the expression of strong opinions in parliament; and strong opinions in parliament, held conscientiously and honestly, should always receive the attention of this chamber and always will.
The Prime Minister mentioned that this is not the first time there have been lengthy debates. I think of the debates of 1910 and 1911, and again in 1912, when for weeks and months on end parliament debated. Indeed, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen received from Sir Wilfrid Laurier the highest tribute that could come from one great parliamentarian to another. Sir Wilfrid on more than one occasion spoke for Liberalism and what it stood for. He held that men should express themselves forcefully and at length. Indeed, he pointed out that the opposition in 1885, in 1896, and again in 1910, 1911 and 1912, on each and every occasion had stood firm for what it believed represented the opinion of many Canadians, and ultimately brought about in the crucible of discussion either an alternative being offered by the government, or on two occasions, election campaigns which entirely supported the opposition and

the stand that it took for a long period of time.
We are not here to decide, and I hope we never will have to decide, the question on a national flag for Canada in a grand assize of the people. We took our stand. The Prime Minister has set out the agreement arrived at today. I was one who from the beginning felt-I say this in no partisan sense, having before me at all times, as has the Prime Minister, the need of preserving, maintaining and conserving unity in the country- that this was a matter that might well have come before a committee as was the case in 1945 and 1946.
I think the first hon. member to suggest a committee was the hon. member for London, on July 2. On July 22 in the course of a television appearance on "The Nation's Business" I asked the question why there should not be a committee. At that time I suggested a committee of both houses of parliament such as had been set up by Mr. King, so that in calmness and with no political bias a recommendation for a flag could be made.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle dealt with this matter at length, and I personally brought before the leaders on the 18th day of August, the suggestion of a committee. I am not going to burden the house with my notes in that regard, but on August 20 I made the suggestion of 15 members, representative of the various parties in accordance with the formula placed before the house by the Prime Minister.
But as the Prime Minister has stated, the meetings among the party leaders did not bring a solution to this problem, in that some felt that whatever recommendation was reached by such a committee should be accepted by the house with a mere token debate or, one might say, with a merely formal and controlled discussion. Our view has been consistent that such a committee should be set up. I would hope that what the Prime Minister has said will be achieved, namely that the committee will produce a recommendation for a flag on the basis of a virtually unanimous decision. After all, flags cannot be imposed.
While fighting strongly throughout for what I believe to be right, in the interests of our country my foremost consideration at all times has been to conciliate, and in what we have achieved here there has been a measure of agreement that I am sure will cause members of the house as a whole to

congratulate themselves on belonging to a chamber that could bring about so complete an agreement.
I was one who believed that the committee would have to meet for some three months of discussion, because this is not something that can be brought about simply by putting a slug in a slot machine and turning out a flag or, in other words, giving a direction to a committee and achieving an instant flag.
I want to make myself perfectly clear, that so far as the Conservative members are concerned they are going into that committee entirely free to come to that conclusion which in their individual opinion is for the benefit of Canada, our first consideration. I do not like in camera meetings in general. However, in this case I am in agreement. If we have an open meeting no one can change his opinion without receiving honourable mention both in the press and over the radio. In other words, whatever position is taken by a member at the first meeting or the first time he speaks becomes a question of history and the record will speak, while you can sit down and exchange opinions, moved by patriotic purpose. I am sure that sitting together for six weeks an agreement should be reached.
Now, I want to say this. While no limitation will be placed on the committee in advance, we in this party are unchanged in our view that unless 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the committee are in agreement we could not, consistent with our consciences and our responsibilities as members, agree to accept a recommendation from the committee without full and untrammelled debate in this house. The Prime Minister said that after the committee has made its recommendation the leaders will endeavour to determine the length of time to be allotted to the debate following that recommendation. I put in this proviso, and I make this very clear, not for the purpose of holding this up in any way. Our view is that the report of a committee of parliament which does not represent virtual unanimity cannot be accepted by the opposition as the appropriate occasion to bring about a diminution, reduction or curtailment of debate.
Now, sir, the Prime Minister has stated that there was a large amount of agreement. There has been very little between us for some time except on the question of what should take place after the committee reported. We were able to resolve that and agree in principle. Mention was made of the fact that a resolution will be placed on the order paper.
Canadian Flag
I have not consulted with my party in this regard, although I did consult fully in respect of the questions that were discussed at the leaders' meeting this morning, but I think I speak for them when I say that after the resolution has been prepared-and it is not a difficult resolution to prepare-I see no reason why we would not immediately give our consent to the order to set up the committee without waiting for the period set out in the rules, so the committee might be appointed at an early date.
The next question concerns what the committee might do. I feel there are many Canadians, organized groups and interested people, who would like to make representations, and 1 would hope that the committee, in order to operate effectively, might permit, within a set time, any organization or individual to put forward its or his views. In addition, the committee might consider whatever designs may have a general appeal as an alternative to the one presented by the government. Indeed, I think this committee, though of course it would be for the committee itself to decide, might well build on the committee reports of 1945 and 1946. There is a tremendous volume of material to be found in the records of that committee. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was a member of that committee as was the hon. member for Kootenay West, and they would be able to corroborate what I say, namely that that committee did a great amount of ground work and research which would be available to the committee we are now about to set up if there is general agreement in the house.
Personally I am very pleased at the giant step forward we have made today. I say to the Prime Minister that I was glad to hear his words when he said that a parliament in which arguments are advanced at length should not be subject to the condemnation which, too frequently and without a reading of history, has been heaped on this parliament in recent weeks.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext:
Parliament represents the voice of the people. No one is obstructing parliament who is speaking for a large number of Canadians who would otherwise be voiceless. No political party, however strong it is, can carry on a fight unless what it stands for is straightforward, honest and touches the heartstrings of the people. We have carried on that fight. Now we have come together on a suggestion which we on this side advanced long since. We have had

Canadian Flag
our disagreements on this matter, and they were strongly felt. Now I hope all of us will close ranks and, in that committee, do honour to parliament, do honour to the members composing it, and show those who criticize us that parliament knows what its responsibilities are and that it epitomizes the finest in parliamentary government, and always will.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there will be general relief in Canada that some working agreement has been reached by the party leaders at the meeting held in the Prime Minister's office this morning. I agree with the Prime Minister that there were no bulls present. This was a steering committee.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext: Oh.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext:
Six weeks of almost continuous debate has an enervating effect upon even the most vigorous male members of the bovine species.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will give general approval to the compromise arrangement which has been worked out and which has been placed before us by the Prime Minister. I hope it will not be spoiled by anyone trying to take credit for it, because this proposal came from many members in different parts of the house at different times, and that it will not be damaged by accusations that any party has made a retreat. I have never felt that stubbornness was a civic virtue. In any public issue a measure of compromise is necessary. Some have to make more concessions than others, and I think the greater the concession the greater the credit to those who are willing to make those concessions. Therefore I make a special appeal to the press of this country that there shall be no suggestion that any party has caved in or that anyone has beaten a retreat. Rather let it be said that all the political parties in this house have sought to find a solution in a most difficult situation, and that instead of demonstrating timidity a measure of statesmanship has been shown in reaching this agreement.
I hope the house realizes, as I am sure it does, that we are not out of the woods yet. We are in the position of a man who has signed a note for his debts, a note which will become due in six weeks' time. At that time we shall still have to face the problem which is now before us. I hope the committee will be able to find an answer. We are

placing a great responsibility upon its members, because if after debating this matter off and on for some two and a half months we have not found a solution, it is evident that the committee has a formidable task ahead of it. Yet I feel confident that if they approach this task in a spirit of co-operation and with a flexibility of mind and attitude, they will find a solution. If they cannot we will still face the problem we face now. I am one of those who has suggested all along that there ought to be a limit on the debate if there is not virtually a unanimous decision, but I do not think there is any value in arguing about that at the present time, as such arguments may be totally unnecessary if the committee produces a virtually unanimous decision.
I think all of us would want to wish the committee and those appointed to it every success in their endeavours, and to assure them that when they bring back their report they will have our grateful thanks for the work they have done. I trust that the committee and the House of Commons will be able to give Canada something no other parliament has been able to give it, a national flag approved by the parliament of Canada; and I trust when that flag has been approved it will fly over a country where the people are united and strong and have a sense of national pride and national purpose.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that not only the members of this house but the people of Canada will be grateful for the decision that was reached at the leaders' meeting this morning and which has now been announced to us. I am sure likewise that this assignment that we are giving to a committee yet to be appointed is a most grave and important responsibility so far as our nation and this parliament are concerned.
I would like to thank the Prime Minister for his concise, non-partisan, honourable statement regarding that which we had agreed upon earlier today. I think it is that spirit which he evidenced in his remarks that assures us this committee is going to be able to meet its responsibility and bring forth, not a compromise-I do not think that is really the word that should be used-but an answer to the problem which we are concerned with and which the nation expects us to solve.
Certainly we have proved today, as it has been proved many times in the history of our

country, that our politicians, our men responsible for government, have been able to agree in a responsible way on a responsible decision for the good of the country. It is well that we should remind ourselves that no emblem, no flag whatever it is, will in itself establish the meaning and loyalties which a flag should carry to a nation and its people. It is only as those things which people themselves represent and stand for are known and respected, not only to their friends but to themselves, that the emblems and flag of a nation can be held in the regard and esteem that they should be. In other words it is not a flag that makes a nation; it is a nation that makes a flag, and this likewise applies to parliament. It is actions, not words, that truly prove what a nation is, and likewise this is true of its people.
We have placed a great responsibility on this committee, not only to decide what the future flag of Canada should be but also to redeem some of the public's respect that this institution has lost during the last few weeks of this debate. I do not think at this point it is necessary to remark further upon the decisions or underline our interpretations of what those decisions mean. Suffice it to say that we in this party will co-operate in every way possible to make the work of the committee constructive and responsible. We look forward with optimism to substantial agreement in the committee, and this in such a way that when its report comes back to parliament it will require only a minimum of debate. In that way we will prove that parliament can act and fulfil its responsibilities as those who elected its members expect it to act.

subtopic: AGREEMENT OF PARTY LEADERS RESPECTING COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with real pleasure that I heard the Prime Minister announce, awhile ago, that at last they had been able to agree on certain points this morning. It may be that my absence was beneficial to that meeting but my reason was already known since I stated, following the last meeting of the five party leaders, that I would no longer attend such meetings. It is not that we wanted to block the adoption of a flag; far from it. The stand taken by the Ralliement Creditiste is very well known to the Prime Minister, to the Leader of the Opposition and to the other party leaders. Our position is that we will not oppose the adoption of a distinctive national flag. That is our stand.
Canadian Flag
Mr. Speaker, day before yesterday my colleague from Megantic (Mr. Langlois) suggested, in his speech, the setting-up of a 15 member committee, exactly what was proposed, a moment ago, by the leader of the official opposition.
We also asked that this committee consider the question for 60 days. This morning there was agreement on six weeks. It is even better.
This committee will be made up of seven Liberals, five Conservatives, one member of the New Democratic party, one Social Credit member and one member of the Ralliement Creditiste. I trust that each member of this parliamentary committee that we are going to establish will have at heart not the past, but the future of Canada. Consequently I would suggest that all parties avoid appointing old fogies to the committee. Let us choose young men, people who have their whole lives before them and who can contribute to the building of our country in the years to come. Thus it would be possible to get the unanimity that the Leader of the Opposition insists upon; considering all that has been said here during the past six weeks, it is obvious that there are still old-fashioned people in Canada. Unfortunately, there are people who turn their eyes to the past instead of looking toward the future.
That is why I would suggest that as many young people as possible be appointed to the committee:	young Liberals, young Conservatives, a young New Democrat, a young Social Crediter and a young member of the Ralliement Creditiste. As far as our party is concerned, there is no problem; it is entirely made up of young people, and that is why we can confidently think of Canada's future.
The Leader of the Opposition said that parliament represented the voice of the people. That is precisely what we have been trying to make clear to the whole house for several weeks:	parliament represents the
voice of the people.
That is why when the Prime Minister decided on a free vote we stated that a free majority vote would necessarily represent the majority opinion of the Canadian people right here in parliament. Why has a free vote not been accepted? In order to prevent the majority from thrusting its opinion on the minority, but we are told, nevertheless, that parliament represents the voice of the people. Then a retreat is sounded and it is suggested once again in parliament that a committee be established. We are told: We shall see in

Canadian Flag
six weeks; another meeting of party leaders will be held to decide whether the debate will be restricted or not. Then, we might find ourselves at our starting point, but I hope not.
That is why I express, once again, the wish that this committee be made up of young members who look to Canada's future, not in terms of a province or a feeling, but of a sovereign country, able to decide by itself what it must do in order to develop and to fulfil itself.

Mr. Speaker, we hope that this very important issue of the national flag will be solved as soon as possible. I think that we will thus show the people as a whole that we are thinking of them and not only of quarrelling as we have been doing for several weeks in this house.
Mr. Speaker, the Ralliement Creditiste will not object to the choice of a distinctive national flag. We will support the report of the committee which will recommend a distinctive national flag, because as Canadians we want to be recognized throughout the world as Canadians with our own symbols.

MR. SCOTT    PRESENCE IN HOUSE DURING VOTE ON FLAG DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I could ask the indulgence of the house on a point of personal privilege. In a story in last night's Toronto Star headed "Nine Toronto M.P.'s miss flag vote" I am listed among the group of Toronto M.P.'s who were absent on Tuesday night for the vote on the motion to adjourn the flag debate. I have in my hand Hansard for Tuesday, September 8 and on page 7736 the record shows that I was present and voted in favour of adjourning the debate.
I am quite prepared to accept responsibility in my constituency for any votes for which I am absent, but I do object to being reported absent when I am in fact in attendance in the chamber. I am satisfied that this was an inadvertent mistake by the reporter. At the same time such mistakes are damaging; and although retractions can never catch up to the original statement, I trust the newspaper in question will take some action to correct the error and the impression it conveyed to its many readers in Danforth riding.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the statement of the secretary general of the United Nations, Mr. U Thant, that the financial crisis as far as the peace keeping forces

Inquiries of the Ministry of the UN are concerned, is rapidly coming to a critical point, and as this relates also to the peace keeping forces in Cyprus, can the minister give us some information in respect of the first question about the over-all picture, and more specifically about what is happening in relation to the Cyprus peace keeping force?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FINANCIAL DIFFICULTIES RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated yesterday that the secretary general is to make a report to the security council with his proposals for the United Nations peace force in Cyprus within the course of the next few days. Until that report is made I am not in a position to comment as to future intentions.
With regard to the financial situation, I fully concur in the statement made by the secretary general yesterday, speaking to the 21 member working group set up to deal with the financing of the United Nations. Canada is a member of that committee, and the government has instructed its spokesmen on that committee to take every step they can to bring about a solution. The government believes that article 19 of the charter is automatic, and that the failure of a country to extricate itself from the application of that article means that it would lose its vote at the general assembly.

subtopic: FINANCIAL DIFFICULTIES RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING OPERATIONS

Last Thursday I asked the Prime Minister, in the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, whether any other nations other than the United Kingdom had undertaken to provide any part of the $2 million that the secretary general has indicated is the minimum requirement to maintain the peace keeping force in Cyprus. I wonder whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs can tell us now if any other nation has undertaken to provide some of this $2 million.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speechtext: 1. Departmental administration, $2,099,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Department of National Health and Welfare is asking parliament to approve expenditures of more than $1-1- billion for the year 1964-65. This represents an increase of 4.9 per cent over our budget for last year, and I think this might be an appropriate time to review some of the department's activities, past, present and future, notwithstanding the fact that for more than two days now hon. members have had an opportunity to go over some of the department's estimates while dealing with interim supply.
Before doing so, however, I should perhaps remind hon. members that as usual the total shown in the estimates does not include an appropriation for payments under the Old Age Security Act. It will be noted that the blue book shows on page 5 anticipated expenditures of another $882 million from the old age security fund. This means that altogether my department expects to spend something more than $2 billion in the current year. It means also, Mr. Chairman, that the department is busier than it has ever been in the 20 years since it was reconstituted from the old pensions and national health department.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Order, please; it is very difficult to hear the minister who has the floor now, particularly in view of the fact that the two ministers in front of her are speaking into the same microphone.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I think we both should make public apologies to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
In both its main branches, health and welfare, important strides are being taken to ensure to all Canadians the highest standards of health throughout their lives, as well as adequate protection for the years during which, for reasons of age or infirmity, they are no longer able to work.
In all our efforts to date, Mr. Chairman, we have maintained an ever closer liaison with our counterparts in the provincial government, and I am sure this co-operation will continue to grow as time goes on. This coordination of effort with the provinces has been aptly called "co-operative federalism" and nowhere has it been more in evidence than in the fields of health and welfare. So far during my term as minister we have had

Supply-Health and Welfare no fewer than seven meetings with provincial ministers holding one or other of these portfolios.
These conferences started with the one which was held on July 25 and July 26, 1963, at which the Canada pension plan proposals and the municipal loans legislation were studied. A further conference on September 9 and 10 of last year was called to deal with the Canada pension plan. From November 26 to November 29 a federal-provincial meeting of premiers was held at which various matters in both the health and welfare fields were discussed. Almost concurrently with these meetings we held our first conference on smoking and health.
Hon. members will also recall the Quebec meetings held at the end of March and beginning of April of this year, at which the various cost sharing programs came under close scrutiny. On May 28 and 29 another fruitful conference of ministers of welfare was held, at which careful study was given to the various public assistance programs. Finally, Mr. Chairman, I met with my provincial counterparts on the health side on July 20 and 21, and I have recently reported to the house on this.
I would not pretend for a minute, sir, that there has always been complete agreement or that the road has not had its bumps. Hon. members are well aware that the federal government has not always been able to do precisely what it originally set out to do or precisely when it intended to do it. We have sought the views of the provinces in areas of mutual concern and jurisdiction, and they have sought ours. But if there have been differences as to approach or method, there has been no difference in the ultimate objective- the highest possible standards of health and welfare for all Canadians. That will continue to be the goal; and if the same spirit of give and take which has marked our endeavours so far continues to prevail as I am sure it will, then we can all look forward to even greater accomplishments in the future.
Mr. Chairman, these 1964-65 estimates do not include provision for expenditures related to the implementation of the Canada pension plan nor to any matter arising from the tabling of the first volume of the report of the royal commission on health services. As hon. members are aware, we expect to have legislation respecting the former before the house during this present session. It remains our intention to have the plan in operation on January 1, 1966.

A national health plan, of course, is another story. Before any legislative proposals can be made in this respect, long and careful study must be given to the report of the Hall commission. At this moment, in fact, some 14 committees in my department are engaged in a most comprehensive examination of the commission's proposals contained in the first volume.
It is expected that our own analysis should be completed in time to present the general position of the federal government to a federal-provincial conference by early next year. I intend to keep the house informed on this subject, as the proposals provide a comprehensive review of the health field, with a basic objective of providing the best possible health care for all Canadians.
I might mention in passing, sir, that in this matter, as in others involving my department in the past, we have been accused by some of moving too fast; by others, of moving too slowly. I suppose this is to be expected and I would simply like to assure hon. members that the government intends to push ahead with the greatest dispatch consistent with sound planning. Our progress may also depend on other factors, including co-operation from all hon. members on both sides of this house.
There are many other important health matters which I am sure will be raised in the discussion of the estimates of my department. For example, I place a great deal of importance on the forthcoming federal-provincial conference on mental retardation. A steering committee has just about completed arrangements for the conference, and the provinces are all co-operating most enthusiastically. It should provide an opportunity for a thorough discussion and assessment of programs for dealing with mental retardation in Canada, with suitable recommendations for future action. In particular, responsibilities of the various agencies in this field will be considered with a view to the co-ordination and integration of effective arrangements for the retarded.
The meeting will be held October 19 to 22, and it is expected that it will bring together 150 persons very closely identified with services for the retarded. These will include representatives from several agencies of the federal government, provincial departments such as health, welfare, education and labour, and representatives from various professional and voluntary associations with special interests and competence in the field. I would hope the conference would lead to greatly improved

provisions for the retarded in Canada, and that future programs would develop on a coordinated and planned basis. Our intentions in this area, incidentally, constitute an interesting parallel with similar programs in the United States, so notably stimulated and encouraged by the late President Kennedy.
Another health program which I would like to mention and which is indicative of important developments in the health fields supported by my department is the one concerning the health hazards of cigarette smoking. Hon. members will recall that at the first Canadian conference on smoking and health, last November, interested federal and provincial health departments and professional and voluntary health organizations agreed that a nation-wide program was necessary to discourage the cigarette smoking habit in Canada, particularly among young people. Federal funds were allotted in the amount of $600,000 to be spread over five years, $400,000 for health education and $200,000 for research.
The Department of National Health and Welfare is endeavouring to provide leadership by assisting in the co-ordination of activities of the various government and nongovernment agencies, by producing basic educational materials for use across the country, and by promoting research into the extent and nature of the smoking habit in Canada and the motivational aspects of smoking.
Two technical advisory committees have been established, one on health education and the other on research. A reference book and an information kit have recently been prepared and distributed. The program of support for research has attracted 19 inquiries from universities in seven provinces, and four projects have already been approved. Also we plan to assist in the distribution of a number of interesting films on the subject. I might add here that the results we have seen so far do not point to any dramatic advance. Our statistics follow rather an erratic pattern, but I am happy to report that the net result is one of slow but steady progress.
The co-operation of the various interested groups has been splendid. An expanded meeting of the technical advisory committee on health education this month will facilitate even wider participation in this program by health workers and educators.
In the field of food and drug control, hon. members will recall that our food and drug regulations have been strengthened during the past year by the promulgation of new control measures. These deal with such matters as the introduction, control and assessment of
Supply-Health and Welfare new drugs; establishment of minimum standards for milk to be used for manufacturing purposes; the addition of several drugs to the list of those which may be sold only on prescription; minimum processing requirements for fish products in hermetically sealed containers to reduce the dangers of botuline poisoning; minimum standards for manufacturing facilities and analytical controls and records required for the manufacture of drugs; standards for live, oral polio virus vaccine; and the distribution of samples of drugs to the medical, dental, veterinary and pharmaceutical professions.
The funds proposed will provide for the inspection, analytical, research and administrative services required to administer this legislation and provide a reasonable degree of protection to Canadian consumers.
This requires that the number of personnel engaged in this work and other facilities be increased to keep pace with the steadily increasing volume and complexity of new processes and new products.
Hon. members will recall that we recently set up an advisory council of consumers which will advise me and my department on subjects related to our food and drug regulations. The committee will hold its first meeting here on October 13 and 14.
If I can turn now, Mr. Chairman, to the activities of our welfare branch, I think this is an opportune time to give members a progress report on the implementation of our new youth allowances program which was passed by the house in July of this year. This particular legislation, which features a somewhat different approach than family allowances, provides for the payment to parents of an allowance of $10 per month for a dependant child aged 16 or 17 who is either in full time attendance at school or university or who is unable to attend school because of a physical or mental infirmity.
The youth allowances act is being administered by the family allowances and old age security division of my department. Since its passage the department has been busy forwarding youth allowances application forms to all parents in Canada who have children aged 16 or 17. It was possible to locate the names of the families concerned from our family allowance records. Some half million application forms were sent out to parents across Canada for September 1. These have already started to flow back into our regional offices in the capital cities of the provinces. As of today I am advised that very few problems are being encountered, so

Supply-Health and Welfare there appears to be every expectation that youth allowances cheques will go forward to eligible parents at the end of this month.
In a situation where a child is unable to attend school because of a mental or physical disability, the parent in question will be sent a certificate which must be completed by a doctor, attesting to the fact that the child is incapable of attending school.
There will be a number of cases where the application form will not reach the parent due to a change of address having taken place since the parent stopped receiving family allowances for the child. Through the use of newspaper advertisements and radio spot announcements, parents who did not receive application forms have been requested to write to their regional director for these forms. All the periodical press of the country, including the ethnic press, has been used for this purpose. Parents whose applications are late because of having to obtain medical certificates, or due to the form not having been received by September 1, will not be penalized by any loss of allowance because of the retroactive provision in the legislation.
Due to the requirement that the youth must be in full time attendance at school, we obviously need the co-operation of the provincial education authorities involved. I am happy to report that I wrote to all the provincial ministers of education, and that the response we have received so far has been most encouraging.
The province of Quebec is continuing its own program, which was initiated in 1960, and will receive from the federal government a fiscal equivalent provided for in the federal-provincial revision act.
It is anticipated that 375,000 children will be registered for the allowance. This will cost some $27 million for the remainder of the current fiscal year. In the full year it is expected the cost will be in the order of $45 million.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word about our public assistance programs. The department has been giving close attention to the four federal-provincial public assistance programs; that is, the three so-called categorical programs of old age assistance, blind persons allowances and disabled persons allowances, and general assistance provided under the Unemployment Assistance Act. Together, these four programs involve an annual federal expenditure of nearly $190 million, and provide basic or supplementary assistance for some 800,000 persons. While these programs are of incalculable


value in providing the essentials of life to those covered by them, questions have been raised for some time about methods of arriving at a better integrated and more flexible public assistance program.
At the federal-provincial conference of premiers last November there was a unanimous agreement that efforts should be made with this objective in view. Accordingly a working group of federal-provincial officials met in February, and the ministers of welfare met with me in May to discuss means of achieving this goal. A further meeting of ministers is planned for later this fall. This sort of action is slow, since it involves the co-operation of the provinces, territories and the federal government and we are all working at different paces, but we are moving forward as quickly as possible.
Among the points brought out in the discussions with the provinces was the fact that the approach taken in the Unemployment Insurance Act, through which the provinces set the rates and determine the conditions under which assistance is granted, should form the basis of any broader public assistance programs that may be developed. Emphasis was also placed on the development of an assistance program designed to encourage self support and the reduction of dependency. The welfare grants program has a role to play in promoting the development and sharing in the costs of social services needed to give this positive emphasis to the public assistance programs.
While much of the discussion with the provinces was concerned with the development of a broader public assistance program, the need for the retention of the present categorical assistance programs on an optional basis by the provinces was emphasized. Accordingly, improvements in these individual programs must also be considered. In particular the program of allowances for people who are permanently and totally disabled needs to be reviewed in the light of the views expressed by many members of this house, as well as in the light of the provisions for disability benefits which are proposed under the Canada pension plan.
It is to be hoped that the federal and provincial governments can work out a mutually satisfactory approach to public assistance, and that the social insurance provisions of the Canada pension plan will be paralleled by an integrated and improved social assistance program.
I might add here, Mr. Chairman, that the welfare grants program continues its planned

expansion as a means of assisting in the development and strengthening of welfare services in Canada. This year $1 million has been allocated to the program, compared with $500,000 in the fiscal year 1963-64. Present plans call for an annual increase of $500,000 until a yearly total of $2J- million is reached.
The program achieves its purpose in a broad and flexible way, partly through directly administered provisions and partly through sharing arrangements with the provinces. Efforts are focused in three main areas; the improvement of the quality and quantity of welfare staff, the expansion of welfare services, and research which holds promise of great improvement in welfare services.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, a word about a program which is small in cost but great in public interest; that is, fitness and amateur sport. The amount made available to us was raised this year to $3 million. Although it is too soon to make any final evaluation of the impact the program is having on fitness and amateur sport in Canada, there is a mounting volume of evidence that considerable progress is being made in a number of the important parts of the program. More than $1 million was allocated in grants to 43 national sports governing bodies and fitness agencies, and 56 per cent of this amount was for training of coaches and participants. About 25 per cent went for assistance to national competition and 15 per cent to international competition.
A sum of $1 million was allocated to the provinces to assist them in developing the services at the local community level which are the lifeblood of the program. Grants are made on a basis whereby the federal government pays 60 per cent and the provinces 40 per cent, except in the case of undergraduate scholarships and bursaries where the federal government pays the full amount. We have been able within the past month or two to offer to the provinces new three year agreements, and we are now negotiating with the provinces on this basis. Up to this time the agreements have been for one year only, and there have been many complaints by the provinces that it was impossible to plan ahead on such a short term basis.
The remaining funds were used for a postgraduate scholarship program through which assistance was given to the training of highly qualified teaching personnel, to fitness research where the co-operation of the universities is being received in the build up of a program that will help to tell us more about the nature of fitness, and to a technical information services program which includes
Supply-Health and Welfare films, manuals of instruction and other techniques for raising sporting skills. The program has not been used to assist capital development because the sums involved are far too great for a $3 million appropriation. However, the department does maintain liaison with the Department of Labour, and through the municipal winter works incentive program the department provides aid for the construction of local sports and recreational facilities.
I have only touched, Mr. Chairman, on some of the highlights of the activities of the Department of National Health and Welfare. There are all told some 29 divisions in the department, and it would take a very long time indeed to give the committee a detailed report on each and every one of them. I have been minister of the department for about 15 months, and daily I encounter a new twist or quirk, a new office or some personnel under my responsibility. I have enjoyed my work. I have enjoyed the people with whom I work.
In concluding I should particularly like to mention the departmental secretary, Miss Olive Waters, who is seated on the floor of the house at the moment, who is the first woman to appear on the floor on the occasion of my estimates to advise me and who, I am sorry to say, is concluding her last year with the department. I should also like to thank the house for the courteous treatment they have given me-except for the first 30 seconds-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister has requested the expeditious passage of her estimates, and I am sure she can count on this. As will be recalled, on July 28 last at the time of our consideration of interim supply we spent a full day discussing the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Many of the members of the party to which I have the honour to belong spoke at that time; and subsequently, under some pressure, the minister did reply on August 5 to some of the questions which were asked. As a consequence we feel that these estimates have been discussed already to some degree. While there will be a few things that my colleagues, and others in other parties, will no doubt wish to comment upon, I

Supply-Health and Welfare do not anticipate any lengthy debate at this stage as far as we are concerned.
The minister, as she put it, touched on the highlights in the department and mentioned that she was meeting new problems every day. I well recall asking a former deputy minister of the department, after having been minister myself for some few weeks, when a person would ever get to feel as though he really might know something about this department. His rather glib reply to me was "Oh, about three years". So I can assure the minister that she has some little time to go, according to this former deputy minister, before she should have everything at her fingertips.
The minister has mentioned the amount Which is being spent. I think something over $2 billion has been devoted to the department including old age security. Eight years ago, if I recall correctly, in 1956-57 the total expenditures including old age security were something in the neighbourhood of $880 million. So the expenditure this year represents more than a 100 per cent increase, 110 per cent to 115 per cent. I know it is money well spent in, as the minister said, an endeavour to provide higher standards of health and life for the citizens of Canada.
At some time when the minister is replying I hope she will give us some indication of just what is happening with regard to the cost sharing programs with the provinces. The Prime Minister tabled letters in this respect today. I have not seen them as yet, and perhaps they will set out the proposals in some detail.
The minister mentioned that she has been having a very busy time with seven dominion-provincial meetings. I feel she would probably have to agree that a couple of those meetings were pretty useless when you look back on them. I am thinking of the July, 1963 meeting and the December, 1963 meeting dealing with the Canada pension plan, which has undergone so many changes.
I do want to commend the minister for the steps she has been taking concerning mental retardation. The forthcoming conference cannot help but be of assistance in this respect, as this illness is a serious matter affecting many people in Canada.
The minister also mentioned the food and drug regulations have been strengthened and which is a good thing. With regard to the advisory council of consumers, we will have to wait and see what comes out of it.
The youth allowances program, as she mentioned, while a little late appears to be


getting under way at this stage, and I am pleased to note that she suggested there were few problems encountered thus far.
With regard to the public assistance program I wonder whether the minister at some stage would indicate whether she has had any suggestions, particularly from the province of Saskatchewan. It occurs to me there is a move afoot out there to suggest that unemployment assistance only be paid in return for work, or perhaps I should say that work should be done in return for public assistance. I wonder whether the minister has any comments on that point.
I should also like to ask her what is the state of the present welfare council, or the welfare council authorized by the previous government. She mentioned the grants being advanced amounting to $500,000, which I recall was the plan devised and which has been followed. This amount is being increased by $500,000 a year until $2.5 million is reached.
The fitness and amateur sport program, which carries the statutory figure of $5 million, is being increased by actual expenditures from $2 million to $3 million this year. I realize that this program cannot be hurried into because the department must make sure that the expenditures are worthy and meet the requirements intended for them. The expenditures have to be studied very carefully, and as a consequence the department cannot leap into a program like this too hurriedly. In other words it must feel its way.
I do not propose to say anything more at this stage, Mr. Chairman. Possibly there will be further questions when we get into the items. However, if I might be permitted one word of commendation to Miss Waters, I should like to join in the minister's words in this respect and wish her well.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope it is a good omen that we are dealing with the estimates of this department sooner than we expected. Granted, this is only a matter of 24 hours, but it is a welcome change from the long delays we are experiencing in respect of some of the important legislative items that the Minister of National Health and Welfare should be bringing before us.
I want to say also that we think it is not inappropriate for the minister to refer to the total amount of money which is provided by parliament for expenditure by or through her department, because this does indicate not only the importance of the work of the department but the tremendous importance

of the subjects covered and the efforts that are made under the aegis of this department to cope with the very real needs of the Canadian people. The minister used the round figure of something over $2 billion as the total amount spent by this department. If my arithmetic is a little more accurate than it was the other day, when I asked her a question about a minor point, that is nearly 30 per cent of the total money spent in a year by the federal government. This indicates that Canadians regard the health, social security and general welfare of our people as one of the most important functions of government.
I should like to make one slight correction in the wording used by the minister, and I do so not to quarrel with her over a technicality, but rather to make a point. If I heard her correctly she said that her department was asking parliament to approve of the expenditure of approximately $1,250 million. Then she went on to refer to the $800 million that came out of the old age security fund, making a total of over $2 billion. I am sure she knows what I am referring to. Actually she comes before parliament asking for approval in respect of only $104 million, for something over $1 billion does not have to be approved by parliament from year to year, because this has been made statutory in the various enactments such as the Old Age Security Act, the Family Allowances Act, and other measures. As I have said, I mention this fact not to quarrel over a technicality with the minister, but rather to make the point that parliament is very sure of itself in this field. It has made permanent enactments which make it clear that we regard social security, social welfare and the health of our people as of major importance in the whole scheme of government as we know it in this country.
We were pleased to hear the report of the minister in respect of the wide range of work that is being done by this department. We were pleased to hear of the extent of cooperation that she and her department experience with the governments and corresponding departments of the provinces of Canada. We were also pleased to learn of the work that is going on inside her department, particularly that being conducted by a number of committees.
I suppose, since I am commenting on some of the things the minister has said, I had better not overlook one point or it might be noticed. I do say very genuinely, at any rate, that I should like to join with the minister
Supply-Health and Welfare and the former minister in complimenting the department for having the services of Miss Waters. Perhaps Miss Waters would not mind if the two deputy ministers who are sitting at the table in front of the minister might also be mentioned as contributing very effectively to the work of this department.
Mr. Chairman, it was good to hear the minister say today that it is still the intention of the government that the Canada pension plan will be brought into effect and be operative by January, 1966. I do not want to sound cynical or lacking in faith; I do not want to sound as though I had not paid heed to the advice of the minister that I possess my soul in patience, or whatever the advice has been from the minister. But, I do express concern as a result of all the delays we have experienced as to whether or not we are going to get this important legislation.
In the short period of time I had earlier today, because word did get around that we might have health and welfare estimates before us this afternoon, I looked over some of the debates of the past, earlier this year and last year, and I found it almost embarrassing to read some of the things that I said as long ago as July, 1963. The things I said then in respect of the Canada pension plan would make one think that the millennium was just around the corner. In the meantime we have had so many delays that one wonders whether that millennium is going to be a millennium in coming. I plead with the minister not to feel that she can put us off from day to day with statements such as, "a statement will be made soon" or "everybody is working on this matter as fast as possible".
Earlier today, when we were on orders of the day, I was quite serious when I made the point that the business of this house, now that we have got over the flag impasse for six weeks, should be organized so that we can get on with the Canada pension plan right away. In my view we should be at it not later than next week. One of the reasons I expressed myself earlier today as opposed to the House of Commons taking a recess at this time is because of the importance of the Canada pension plan itself. I favour a recess for our staff, and I think that it can be worked out, indeed, we must work it out; but we have been telling the country for a long time that we have felt there was important business for us to get at, and for that reason we wanted some agreement made about the flag debate. Let us not spoil all that by asking now for a holiday, when there is this important question of the Canada pension plan, as well as other important business to be dealt with at this time.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not need to be out of order to answer that question, because I answered it by what I said about 90 seconds ago.
So far as the Canada pension plan is concerned, Mr. Chairman, this is one of the responsibilities of this department, and one of the items to which the minister herself referred in her opening statement. I suggest to her that it is not sufficient for us to be willing to stay here to deal with it, but what has to be done is to have the legislation brought before us. We are glad that we were given the white paper some time ago-on August 10 I believe it was. It is an excellent document which probably tells us more than the members generally will be able to comprehend when they receive the bill itself, because I expect the bill will be so complicated we will all readily agree to give it second reading and refer it to a committee. I do not think we will be able to discuss it here, because of its tremendous complications.
Mr. Chairman, the minister's responsibility is to get that piece of legislation before us. I ask her to consider what is happening to the calendar. We are well into the month of September and if I can count months it is only a little over three months until Christmas. It is not impossible, even with the kind of accord and agreement we have reached in parliament today, for other roadblocks to occur, for other matters to be debated at length and for this important piece of legislation to be put off again and again. It is not impossible for other difficulties to arise in discussions with the provinces. It is not impossible for difficulties to arise when the matter goes before a special joint committee. These various difficulties could add up to the postponing of this legislation into 1965, and if that happens it is quite possible that the intention the minister stated today could fail to be realized.

This is an important matter not just to the Liberal party which campaigned so heavily on it in the last two elections. It is also an important matter to parliament and it is an extremely important matter to the people of Canada. Judging from the white paper and from all we have heard and read about the matter, it strikes me that a great many people have put much thought into this plan. We will probably find some flaws in it, some things that we want to improve, but generally it strikes me as a good piece of social legislation, and what is now needed is that we get it on the statute books. Before we know it other parliamentary crises could arise. There could even be an election next year or the year following. By this sort of thing these benefits could be denied to many people who are waiting for them and who are entitled to them.
So I urge the minister to get the resolution respecting the Canada pension plan on the order paper next week, and I offer her this bit of co-operation. I am one of those persons who attend meetings of the house leaders where we try to organize the business of the house, and I tell her, though she knows it very well, that the minute the resolution preceding the Canada pension plan is on the order paper I will be pleading with her house leader and the other house leaders that we give it the very highest priority. We cannot do that at the meetings of house leaders if the legislation is not on the order paper.
Because we have got the white paper on the Canada pension plan one could go into some of its details, but I will resist that temptation. I will wait hopefully for that debate next week. But there is one thing in the pension field with regard to older people which I feel I must press upon the minister. I asked her a question the other day arising out of a resolution passed by the united senior citizens of Ontario. She took the question seriously and it was a serious question, but a colleague in the party to my right referred to it as though it was a question asked in jest. It certainly was not asked in such a vein.
My question had to do with the request that many people now over 70 and now receiving old age security of $75 a month are asking for an increase in that pension and the figure they are now suggesting is $100 a month, which I support. I know it is very easy to say there was an increase last year and also the year before and that we have done pretty well in the few years since the amount was $40 a month. I know it is easy to say that

we are going to be coping with the whole problem of old age security on the broader basis that is involved in the Canada pension plan, but the fact still remains that there are still many Canadians over 70 and many more who will become 70 before the Canada pension plan comes into effect who have no prospect of anything other than old age security as we now know it. We feel it is not good enough just to make provision to take care of needs in the years that lie ahead. We think we have to consider the needs of our people here and now.
There is no question in my mind that when the Canada pension plan comes into effect and we have this two stage program, old age security and the Canada pension plan, the amount paid under old age security will have to be increased in the course of time and that if the kind of pension we envisage is going to be available a decade or two or three from now the amounts paid under both the Canada pension plan and old age security will have to be increased. Since this is coming anyway, I ask the house to get over the notion that we have seen the end of increases in old age security itself. If we are going to make these increases let us have in mind the older people of the present time, who will rejoice in the knowledge that other people are going to do better as they become older, and let us see to it that we increase old age security now and make things better for them as well while they are still with us.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, I welcome very strongly the minister's statement today that it is still the government's intention to have the Canada pension plan in operation by January, 1966. I welcomed in July the statement of the Minister of Justice that so far as the government was concerned the Canada pension plan would be enacted at this session of parliament. But we have had promises of this kind before over the years. My plea today is that these promises be kept at this session. We promise our full co-operation to get this done and we ask the minister and the government to do their part so far as this whole matter is concerned.
We welcome also the brief review the minister gave of the various other programs in the social welfare field, the categorical programs and the other forms of assistance and social welfare. We are glad to know these programs are constantly being reviewed by the federal government and the provinces. I know that in speaking to the minister I am speaking to one of the converted. I am sure she is even more converted now than 20220-495
Supply-Health and Welfare she was a year ago, having got to know more about the work of her department; but I plead that she press on with the idea of integrating these programs and overcoming the patchwork approach to social security which has been inevitable because of the way the whole matter has grown up.
I also ask that the government realize that social security is not just a form of charity for people who are in need. It is a part of our whole approach to our kind of society in which we believe there is a case for the redistribution of wealth so that people will be enabled to live according to their needs and be able to live according to what society is able to produce. Other departments than the minister's, the Department of Labour in particular, are concerned with the problem of automation.
I listened to a part of the speech the Minister of Labour made in Toronto the other day on this question and since then he has supplied all of us with copies of this speech. It is not surprising to learn that he is concerned about what automation is doing to the processes of collective bargaining and to the employment picture. We are all concerned. This sort of thing hastens the day when governments will have to be concerned not just with providing social security payments of the order we now envisage, but when governments in the name of society will have to be concerned about the distribution of the mass of income that we produce according to the needs of our people rather than in accordance with the industrial or other work they are able to perform. Many a modern economist and sociologist is recognizing the fact that the day may not be far off when we will have to pay people who do not work at all, not through some form of relief but actually pay them to enable them to live and make it possible for them to engage in creative and constructive pursuits. I suggest that this problem concerns not only the Department of Labour but will concern this minister's department because this is the department where we have laid the groundwork for finding ways in which to distribute the wealth we produce among our people.
A few decades ago social legislation was only for the poor. Not very long ago I heard Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King-I think he was sitting in the very seat in which the minister is sitting now-stand up in this house and talk about the needy poor. Even when he used that phrase 20 years ago there were those in this house who castigated him for it. They said, surely we had moved on from that time. Of course Mr. HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare King belonged to an earlier generation and that was reflected in his thinking. This was what social welfare was, simply picking up the pieces, helping to provide an ambulance to pick up those who had suffered in the processes of our society and of our economy. We have moved on from that point and we realize that the maintenance of an adequate standard of living, not just keeping people alive, but enabling them to enjoy the benefits of our age, enabling them to live a constructive life, is one of the goals of our society.
We are going to have to move a great deal farther in that direction in the next decade. There is already co-operation between the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Labour on a number of matters. I think there should be a great deal of study of this whole question of how we can expand the pension, social welfare and assistance programs we have so that our people can live and perform as they ought to, and not suffer from the processes of automation.
There is one other main branch of the minister's department with which I shall deal, and some of my colleagues will be speaking about this is greater detail. I want to say just a few words about it at this point. I refer to the whole question of health which has again been brought into sharp focus by a report. I refer, of course, to the report of the Hall royal commission. We have had many reports and documents in this field in the years that have gone by. The minister recalls that when I was speaking on her estimates last year I drew to her attention a draft bill for a national health program which had been tabled in this House of Commons by one of her predecessors, Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie, back in 1944. I found it a matter of some interest that the minister admitted to me, either publicly or privately and I am sure it does not matter which, that she had not heard of that particular draft bill until I drew it to her attention. This was one of a great many documents. There was the Marsh report and several other huge volumes during the years I have been here, and even before that.
The Hall report is another one and it has brought the whole question of the community's responsibility for the health of our people into sharp focus. We agree that it is an excellent report. Like most reports, it contains one or two things with which we do not entirely agree. But the general call for a health charter for Canadians is one that


all of us welcome most heartily. When one reads this report even sketchily he gets the impression that the members of the commission, who were not New Democratic appointees to start with and who were not socialistic in their thinking, became convinced as they studied the matter that the only answer to the health problem of Canada was a health charter for Canada somewhat along the lines of that spelled out in the report. We hope however this is not going to be just another massive and valuable document that will decorate the shelves of the library and be referred to for years to come.
I welcome the minister's statement that there are 14 committees in her department studying the various aspects of this report. I welcome her statement that it is hoped that this study will have proceeded sufficiently to enable the government to present a position to a federal-provincial meeting some time in 1965. However I strongly express the hope that is not just for the purpose of entertaining those who attend the meeting, but rather that this will be a step in the direction of urging that this legislation be brought into effect. I know that this government has had a rather rough time of it since it got elected. It promised action in 60 days and that 60 day slogan became almost a millstone around its neck. Then the government had trouble with the first Gordon budget. Then there was the Canada pension plan which we were going to get right away, but which we are still hoping to get. Health care was part of the Liberal party's platform in the last election. I believe the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was faced with a Liberal candidate who put the health program so high on the list it was going to be enacted in a matter of months.

speechtext: Do not forget the scholarships.

I urge the government not to be discouraged because it has had this kind of trouble, not to be discouraged to the point of putting the health plan too far down the list. It is perhaps even more important than the Canada pension plan and the minister knows how important we feel that is. If this government or the minister in charge of this department really want to do something for Canada, I suggest they should make a serious effort to get a health charter for Canadians

on the statute books during the life of this parliament.
The impression we get, and I am sure the impression the press men have, including those who are friendly to the Liberal party, is that the most the government plans in this field is to get the pension plan on the books, perhaps the national labour code, and then be able to use that in an election campaign. They would say, you have this and we will go on with a health plan if you reelect us. This is not good enough. This is not acting in a responsible manner. Now that we have the Hall report and this government committeed to act in the health field, I urge that there should be no thought of the health plan being put off for the next parliament, but rather plans should be made to get this legislation before this house during the life of the present parliament. It is a tenuous life this parliament leads. You never know when it is going to fall on some major issue, some minor issue or even some procedural issue. I think the thing for the government to do is to assume it still has life, and while it has that life it should act on these important matters.
There are other things I should like to discuss, but quite frankly I would be repeating what I have said on other occasions about improvements that might be made in the Blind Persons Act and the Disabled Persons Act, unemployment assistance and some of these other things. Some of the programs to which the minister has referred deserve comment. This comment can be made by other members as the debate proceeds. As the minister expected I would, however, I want at this time to urge that she get moving with something more than a Liberal pace, that she get moving with some real speed on these two important matters, the Canada pension plan and a health charter for the people of this country.
