Mr. Chairman, while I do not want to delay the discussion unnecessarily, I would like to make a few remarks on the National Health and Welfare estimates, to call the attention of the house on the fact that at first sight, no extraordinary changes appear in the departmental estimates. Several items have remained the same, whereas some others show a slight increase like, for instance, the contribution to the provinces, following arrangements made between them and the federal government. We also note an increase in medical services. The largest increase con-20220-4954
Supply-Health and Welfare cerns the new estimates for the old age pension plan.
This pension plan will not directly concern the province of Quebec, as Quebec citizens will have their own pension plan, but I may say that even that plan does not inspire much confidence as far as I am concerned, because I consider it simply as a product of capitalism.
When we look at this pension plan, we wonder whether the government really wanted to help old people in need, or come to the rescue of government finance, because under that plan the small wage earner who gets from $1,000 to $6,000 will be taxed again, whereas those in higher brackets will not be affected.
Now, it is precisely the small wage earners who have to raise a family on $3,000, $4,000 or $5,000 a year, who are of concern to us, because they will have to shoulder another tax to be eligible for a pension 25, 30 or 40 years hence.
Mr. Chairman, after having studied every program and every bill which was enacted by the house, I wonder whether there is a true and honest concern for individual welfare. I am asking this question seriously, because since my arrival in this house, it seems to me that all the acts I have studied have been drawn up not in the interest of the individual, but with finance in mind.
I feel that, in setting up the present scheme, the government's chief purpose is to create a tremendous fund where it can dig at will, while luring the people with a pension they could hope to receive when they reach the age of 70.
Mr. Chairman, if the government were really sincere and truly wanted to protect people and our older citizens, it could use a much less complicated means than the pension plan it is now proposing. In fact, we are now paying our old people a pension of $75 a month from the age of 70.
We want our old people to receive a pension of $100 a month, for that is exactly what the new plan proposes, $100 and less-I say "and less", because I find that, under that scheme, the aged person will have to prove that, all his life, he earned a salary of $6,000 a year. Therefore, the person who will establish that he earned only $3,000 a year will receive only $50 per month as stipulated in the proposed plan, and so on. Those who earn only between $3,000 and $4,000 a year will receive a pension in keeping with their salary.
During all that time, the Canadian citizen will have been deprived of the necessities of life in order to have a guaranteed pension of $100. Because the most needy people will not.

Instead of all that camouflage, the government could have raised the present pension from $75 to $100 per month and pay it out of the surplus income of the wealthy without overtaxing the little people.
Those earning $6,000 and over could have been taxed in order to pay for that additional pension of $25 a month. Thus, I think the government would have been much more logical and would have proven that they were working to improve the situation of small wage earners while securing a $100 pension for everybody, including those who have millions of dollars. I think that is a principle of social distribution which is fair and equitable for everybody.
But we have chosen once more to take billions of dollars out of the pockets of the small wage earner to give him a few crumbs when he reaches 70 years of age.
I say that if today with the pension-I see somebody opposite who laughs at the low income people; he should not laugh at them because the father of ten or 12 children earning less than $5,000 a year will be burdened even more as a result of this famous pension plan. Let us not laugh at our small wage earners; instead let us consider their plight more seriously and let us help them by providing them with a more adequate social pension.
If the Minister of National Health and Welfare wishes to bring about some improvements, we could even today pay without a means test a pension to those who have reached 65 years of age, instead of waiting until they are 70.
We could do away with this army of small inspectors, all these branch offices which cost millions of dollars to this department, and with the savings realized by eliminating these petty inspectors-I was about to say those small patronage dispensers-who study the cases of persons 65 to 70 years of age in order to find a way to get out of paying pensions to them, we could pay, without a means test, part of the statutory pension to persons 65 to 70 years of age.
Mr. Chairman, an item which impressed me especially is that of family allowances.
The government provided family allowances several years ago, and I wonder whether the Minister of National Health and Welfare has ever thought of revising them in keeping with the rise in the cost of living.


There is some talk of increasing family allowances; requests are made, large families especially write to the government. But the government pretends not to hear those requests and remains silent when questions are directed to its members in the house concerning the problem of family allowances.
All salaries are increased nowadays, the administration costs have increased; the only item which is left untouched is that of family allowances.
It is precisely the only way to help large families and set a fairer salary balance.
If two family heads receive the same salary, but one has two or three children while the other has ten or more, the only way to balance their salaries is precisely through family allowances.
Again, I wonder if the Minister of National Health and Welfare thought of this. In the estimates, I see only a small increase, which I gather is merely the result of the population increase. But, in fact, there are no changes whatsoever as far as family allowances are concerned. And no changes are announced either, and sometimes I wonder if the minister does not intend to reduce them instead of increasing them.
Mr. Chairman, there are very interesting items in the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and the most interesting of them all, even more interesting than old age pensions, is family allowances.
It is really a shame today to see that a country like Canada is unable to make an effort to help large families balance their budgets through proportionate family allowances, so that they might live like other workers who have little or no family.
I feel that this question must be considered, and I ask the minister to consider it seriously and introduce a few amendments so that we might hope for at least a 100 per cent increase in family allowances. The cost of living has actually more than doubled during the last decade. I feel the time has come to be logical.
If the minister acts along those lines, I think that she will make a useful contribution to Canada's future.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we were all taken by surprise, this afternoon, when the party leaders' decision to set up a committee to study the flag question left us free to discuss the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare. However, since I am sure that those estimates will be approved sometime today and probably early this evening, I should like to say a few

words just to show that we have always been highly interested in that department and that we are always glad to offer a few suggestions to the minister.
In my opinion, the Department of National Health and Welfare, as organized at the present time, is surely the one whose activities do the most to prepare a general election.
I always deplored the fact that both health and social welfare come under the same department. In my opinion, the government should seriously consider dividing that department in two so that health, a matter of the utmost importance for the whole country, will be kept completely apart from another one just as important, social welfare.
Social welfare is indeed very important, although the needs in that field are recognized in general at election time only.
That was obvious several times, when family allowances were granted for the first time and later when various adjustments were made. We know that had been done arbitrarily and at the very last minute, just before an election, because it was realized that the results of that election could depend on votes cast by parents.
Also, it was realized that an increase in old age pensions was granted almost at the same time, in order to profit from the vote of Canada's senior citizens.
Therefore, I think that if this department was split in two, the health of the Canadian citizens would not at all be impaired and the question of social welfare would be studied rationally, systematically and progressively, not only in keeping with the cost of living, but also with the social evolution of the population, and not because of the political implications which such an increase in allowances might have among the Canadian population.
It is noteworthy that little by little various pressures, sometimes very subtle, are exerted by followers of certain political doctrines and also by some newspapermen in their editorials. Thus, our democratic system seems to evolve slowly towards a system against which we fought bitterly in wartime.
We should not deceive ourselves nor think that things which were bad before are now better; because more and more people are hoping for the social welfare state and for the government to play an ever increasing role, we should not think that they are right when they were wrong a few years ago.
It is not because the number of thieves in the country is increasing that the legislation against theft should be amended. The govern-
Supply-Health and Welfare ment should not come to believe that theft is a good thing simply because more thieves are committed. We should not do like certain political partisans who approve of theft when it is in favour of their party but reject it when it is in favour of other groups.
I believe that while it is in order to greet with some hope the establishment of a pension plan or fund for the Canadian people, while it is in order to rejoice at the fact that individuals who benefit from social assistance will perhaps have their day because there will be an election at a given time, I think that we must be very sparing in praising the government.
It must be realized that we are on very slippery ground, that we are implementing schemes which have been tried out in other countries where it has been shown that those so-called liberating plans always bring us back, sooner or later, to systems that become centralizing, dictatorial and detrimental to the people, although they had supposedly been established to help them.
As an example, I will refer only to Great Britain, where a system was established supposedly to satisfy all the needs of the British people-since it is a step forward as regards the existing hospital insurance legislation-* where the health insurance system was to solve all problems; nevertheless, a short time after the implementation of that system, it was realized that the amounts of money invested were getting phenomenal and extravagant, that the operating cost of the system was such that medical care began to decrease, that medical research was practically nonexistent and that hospitalization costs were becoming unbearable to the taxpayer, because, after all, the revenues needed for the maintenance of that whole system are always derived from taxes, in short, the taxpayer has to pay for it.
This means that far from freeing the British people from expenditures incurred through illness, this scheme has made them extraordinarily vulnerable, because the treatments which were supposed to be given at a minimum cost have now reached astronomical figures.
I think that from time to time, committees should be set up, such as the one which will consider the flag issue, in order to ascertain the views of the various parties which, after all, reflect the views of the Canadian people, before launching an ill-considered scheme that we know nothing about. Before being compelled to back down, we might be better advised to consult people

Supply-Health and Welfare and to do more research in this field. Before assuming that exceptionally good results will be achieved, it might be better to follow the example of countries that have used the different systems.
I feel the Canadian people would become more cautious and have second thoughts before insisting on the ill-considered intrusion of the state in the fields of health, welfare and social security.
If I remember correctly certain notions of social science I may have learned, it seems to me that state intervention, no matter how intensive or far reaching should be meant to establish some happy medium among the people and to provide the majority with the basic necessities.
I do not believe that it is by increasing the cost of government services, while decreasing the number of services, that the people can be served.
Therefore, I caution the government, as well as hon. members, not to think that pension plans, health insurance plans and hospital insurance plans will be cure-alls for all our present ills.
It is not because the capitalist system is defective in itself but simply because, in its present application, this system does not take into account hard facts nor its own weaknesses. For fear of having to relinquish some prerogatives, we are unwillingly getting into another plan for which the government is not anxious, against which it once fought, but in which it cannot help but flounder.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to speak at length. In addition to her statement on the Canada pension plan, the minister referred to the research made or co-ordinated by her department with regard to cigarette smoking which is related to metabolic disturbances causing heart trouble and blamed also for its effects on lung cancer.
I feel that the government is to be commended for having accepted its responsibilities in this field. I do not believe, however, that in this respect as in others, the government should give strict orders to all the people, because studies made up to now have failed to show the actual cause or any close relationship between the use of tobacco and lung cancer or cardiovascular diseases.
I also take this opportunity to say a few words on fluoridation. That is another controversial matter which has been considered and discussed without having been unanimously settled.
I do not see how the government could give any directives or definite opinions in

this field, when ideas all over the world differ on the matter.
We should keep in mind that, when the Minister of National Health and Welfare places her authority behind a statement, a medical report or an investigation on a given subject, it has great influence on the public.
I believe that the Department of National Health and Welfare, while supporting the national health league and various other organizations which advocate water fluoridation should limit its activities. It should not increase the various subsidies and more particularly take no decision before the government thoroughly and satisfactorily studies the question. Moreover, the government should note the views expressed by the various scientists of our own national research council.
Mr. Chairman, I would have liked to end my remarks immediately, but since I still have a few comments to make, may I call it five o'clock?

The house resumed from Thursday, August 27, consideration in committee of Bill No. S-27, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada-Mr. Brown-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Number of directors.

Mr. Chairman, as sponsor of Bill No. S-27, I should like to take this opportunity of answering one or two questions which were asked by the hon. member for Greenwood, the hon. member for Timiskaming and others.
I should like to repeat, Mr. Chairman, what I have already said in the course of this debate, that it is the wish of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, through this bill, to increase the number of its directors in order to deal more effectively with the growth and complexity of the diverse problems that confront it in the operation of its business during these times. The committee and the house have already been made aware of the general growth and development of this company since its charter was issued, and particularly since the year 1927 when it began to make use of its full quota of directors. It is the view of the company that the complexity and diversity of matters and problems coming before its board make it desirable at this time to request parliament to grant it an increase in the permissible size of its board of directors, and there is no other reason. I might say there is no other hidden reason behind the company's request to parliament at this time. Nor is there any change in the policies or plans envisaged which might be facilitated by an increase in the size of its board of directors. I wish to state emphatically that it is not the intention of the company to use any additional directors allowed for the purpose of amalgamation or merger with any other company.
The hon. member for Greenwood referred to an application of Industrial Wire and Cable
Private Bills
Company to the board of transport commissioners respecting the relationship between the Bell Telephone Company and the Northern Electric Company, in respect of which a ruling was given that the Bell Telephone Company was legally entitled to own shares in the Northern Electric Company. As hon. members know, the Bell Telephone Company now owns 100 per cent of the shares of the Northern Electric Company.
It was pointed out to the committee that a further question before the board of transport commissioners in this application was never dealt with, namely whether the board was entitled to review the financial affairs of the Northern Electric Company. I believe I have been asked why this question was never considered. I cannot give the answer to that question because this is a matter for the board of transport commissioners. The applicant, namely Industrial Wire and Cable Company, has never asked the board for a hearing on this question. There is nothing to prevent the applicant from asking the board for a hearing at this time, and I am assured that there is no objection from the Bell Telephone Company to its doing so.
With respect to the annual report of the Northern Electric Company, I might state that this annual report is available to any hon. member, at any time, for inspection and can be obtained upon request. It has already been supplied to a number of hon. members who have requested it.
I was further asked whether the Bell Telephone Company would permit some, or one, of the directors to be appointed by the parliament of Canada. It is pointless for me to answer this question. The directors are appointed by the shareholders of the company at the annual meetings of the company. The board of transport commissioners is the institution which has been charged by parliament to protect the public.
Mr. Chairman, I have endeavoured to answer the questions which have been raised in regard to these very important matters as carefully as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I think during the consideration of this bill it would be well for us to review the position of this company and its operations over the last number of years so that we may have a clear idea of what sort of a corporate body we are considering.
The company was incorporated in 1880 under special act of the dominion government as a result of the consolidation of a

Private Bills
number of smaller companies at that time. From then on it began to absorb a number of other companies. In 1954 it merged the former subsidiaries, Eastern Townships Telephone Company and the Chapleau Telephone System. Also in 1954 it absorbed the Welland County Telephone Company. The following year it absorbed the Saguenay-Quebec Telephone Company, and the Charlevoix Telephone Company. In 1956 it merged the Kamaraska Telephone Company, and in 1957 it acquired the Mount Albert Telephone Company. In 1957 it also acquired 272,000 common shares of Northern Electric Company, increased its holdings in this company in 1962, and my latest information is that it is still holding 99 per cent of the common shares. However, there is very little difference between 99 per cent and 100 per cent. In 1959 it merged the Yamaska Telephone Company and in the following year it acquired the Madawaska Telephone Company. In 1962 it acquired control of the Avalon Telephone Company.
I am reciting these facts, Mr. Chairman, not in criticism of the actions of this company, because I think that is the logical method by which a public utility such as a telephone company must operate, because there is no room for competition in this particular field, but to underline the fact that this company has, since 1880, virtually taken over the whole of the telephone business in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. In fact, Moody's Annual states that this company owns and operates the most important telephone system in Quebec and Ontario over an area of 887,000 square miles, serving a population of 11,700,000.
This is a very large proportion of the total population of Canada. I think it is important we should realize this because we can then realize the vital importance of this company and its operations to the people of central Canada. The operations of the company affect the private lives of all individuals who have to have telephones for their own domestic purposes and every business in central Canada is utterly dependant on this company for the efficient communication system it requires. As I say, I am not complaining for the moment about the monopoly position of this company but I want to underline the fact that it is a monopoly and that by the very nature of its business it has been a monopoly.
There have been questions raised with regard to the transactions that take place between the Bell Telephone Company and its almost wholly owned subsidiary, the Northern
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) .1
Electric Company. These questions have had to do with whether or not this may be one method by which the parent company can salt away a large part of its earnings and come within the terms of the rate structure set by the board of transport commissioners. I have no conclusive evidence in this regard but I do have here the annual report of Northern Electric for 1962 which sets out some rather interesting figures. For instance, it tells us that in 1962 this company's cash on hand and in banks was almost 50 per cent higher than it had been in 1961. In 1961 the amount was just over $2 million and in 1962 it was just over $3J million.
But here is the real milk in the coconut. In 1961 short term investments of the Northern Electric Company amounted to only $2,624,000 but by the following year they had increased five times to $11,054,000. It is very obvious that Northern Electric Company is doing extremely well out of its manufacturing of telephone equipment, the vast majority of which, according to the vice president of Bell Telephone, is sold to its parent company, Bell Telephone. If one were of a suspicious nature, which I am far from being, one might imagine that the Bell Telephone Company perhaps found it advantageous to pay to its wholly owned subsidiary rather larger prices for telephone equipment than were normally justified.

speechtext: He knows as well as I do the provisions of the standing order about relevancy and I would invite him to keep that in mind as we proceed.

I will, Mr. Chairman, and you will realize as I go on with what I am saying that my remarks are completely relevant. There are certain matters that I think must be made plain to the committee. The first, and to my mind the most important, is to recognize the monopoly position of this company and the complete dependence of the very large proportion of Canadians who live in central Canada on the operations of the company.
The company has come before us to ask us to authorize the appointment of five new directors. My colleagues in this party have proposed that three of these directors should be appointed by the government or by parlia-

ment as public representatives on the board to keep an eye, if you like, on the public interest in the operations of this company. I think you will agree, Mr. Chairman, that if as we contend this is advisable, then there is one thing these public representatives should also keep a very close eye on, namely the operations of this wholly owned subsidiary, because it may well be that an examination of the books of Northern Electric in conjunction with an examination of the books of the parent company may show that the public interest is not being fully protected in the relationships and the transactions between the parent and subsidiary companies.
I have quoted some figures to suggest, ever so gently, that in the balance sheet presented by the Northern Electric Company there may be some grounds for this doubt and suspicion. For instance, the net earnings of this company, most of whose business is with the Bell Telephone Company, amounted to less than $5J million in 1961 but by the following year its net earnings had reached $8,834,000. That would appear to me to be a matter of very great interest to anyone appointed to the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company to protect the public interest. Therefore I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it is quite relevant to the argument I am presenting for the necessity of having some measure of public control and supervision over companies that are of such vital interest to such a large portion of the population.
My own personal view, of course, which stems quite naturally from my political and economic views, is that this company should be a crown corporation, that it is perfectly ridiculous that something so vital to the welfare of the people of Canada should be left in the hands of private individuals. I think it is nonsensical. I see no particular hope of achieving that end now, but I do think that parliament has a responsibility to consider whether or not it should decide at this point that a company of this size and importance should have some measure of public supervision.
When we discussed this matter with the vice president of the Bell Telephone Company he was rather plaintive. He wanted to know why we were singling out the Bell Telephone Company and why we did not apply the same yardstick to other companies. I said I would be delighted to do so and intended to do so on every occasion that one popped up its head here and rendered itself liable to this sort of treatment, which has been perhaps unfortunate for the Bell Tele-20220-496
Private Bills
phone Company in that they were the first to come to parliament with such a request and were obvious targets for this sort of development-which I really think is one that to most thoughtful people would constitute a very moderate and reasonable demand on the part of our party with regard to the control of this company.
In my discussions with the vice president of the Bell Telephone Company I pointed out to him that such provisions were not unheard of in the world and that there were places where the supervision and direction went much farther. I pointed out, for instance, that in France there is a public director on the board of directors of every bank who, incidentally, has the power of veto over directorial decisions. There are a number of public directors appointed to such industrial operations as the French steel industry in which the public has an investment of only 30 per cent. Obviously it was decided in France that corporations that were important to the welfare of the whole country must be subjected to some measure of public control and public supervision. I think we have been very modest in suggesting that out of these five new directors three should be public representatives, and not demanding that the whole five should be.
I was interested in the remarks made by the vice president to me with regard to not only the purpose in seeking this authorization but the sort of people they had in mind to get. He told me they had in mind people from the academic world. Just what they were going to be doing on a telephone company's board I was not quite sure, but possibly the idea was that they would lend a certain air of intellectual responsibility to the company's operations. But it did occur to me at the time, if the company considers it is in its interests and presumably in the interests of the public to have people from the academic world sitting on the board of directors, how much more important it is that directors should be appointed vested with the responsibility of guarding the public interest, and not just academic interest or whatever interest these people were supposed to be concerned with in the operations of this company. I hope the House of Commons will not pass the bill until it is amended to incorporate the provision that members of this party have advanced in earlier discussions of this matter.

I wanted to ask the sponsor of the bill a question, as to whether or not he had discussed with the Bell Telephone Company directors the request we made for rep-

resentation on the board of members of the government, and if so what was the nature of their response to this request? Are they prepared to entertain the idea or are they turning it down flat?

I endeavoured to answer that question. As the company is set up, the directors are appointed by the shareholders. Unless the law is changed or varied this matter cannot be the subject of discussion here because appointments to the board have to be approved by the shareholders.

That is a technically correct answer. However, it does seem that whoever the board wants to get on the board somehow manages to be elected at the annual meeting. A very small percentage of these shares is being voted under proxies and by some strange process or coincidence, to my knowledge the choice of the administration is always elected to the board. I have not the slightest doubt if your gentleman would give us this assurance, that the nominees of the government would be on the slate, or whatever they call it, we would be happy to have that assurance. I think they can give us the kind of guarantee that would result in these people being elected at a shareholders meeting. I still want to know whether or not they are prepared to consider the idea and give us that assurance.
I could not give that assurance at this time. It was discussed, but as I stated no director is competent to state that the parliament of Canada should appoint a director to the company.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking on previous Thursdays in connection with this Bill S-37 by which the Bell Telephone Company of Canada seeks to increase the number of directors from 15 to 20, I have pointed out that my interest in this bill stems from the fact that a competing company with Northern Electric is located within the riding of York West. The factory or production centre is in the riding of York West, but many of the employees of that company are residents of the riding of York-Humber.
Now, some time ago the hon. member for Timiskaming asked a rhetorical question as to why the Bell Telephone Company wished to increase its directors from 15 to 20. I might state that, personally, I am in favour of increasing the number from 15 to 20 if we should ever get to a vote. However, in answer to the hon. member for Timiskaming 1 should like to suggest that the company wants more directors in order to strengthen

its hold on Northern Electric. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands stated that the Bell Telephone Company controls 99 per cent of the stock of Northern Electric, which company is not under public supervision.
I have in my hands a Hansard, report of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. This is the report of a meeting held on Tuesday, July 7, 1964. Mr. Vincent, the president of the Bell Telephone Company answered a question by one of the hon. members for Halifax which is recorded on page 416 of this report, and I quote:
We own 100 per cent of Northern Electric Company Limited.
There may be some directors with qualifying shares which would not be in the name of the Bell Telephone Company but may be entered in the name of the directors. However, the president of the Bell Telephone Company states that they own 100 per cent of Northern Electric Limited. Then, Mr. Regan, one of the two members for Halifax, questioned the representative of the Bell Telephone Company during this committee meeting. He asked specifically if it was not correct that Bell was entitled to own shares of Northern Electric Company simply because of a certain clause in their charter which states that they can buy any company operating a telephone line. Mr. Venne, who is vice president and general counsel gave the answer which is recorded on page 417 as follows-he is quoting section 4 of the incorporating act:
The company shall also have power to enter into any arrangement with any person or company possessing, as proprietor, any line of telegraphic or telephonic communication, or any power or right to use communication by means of the telephone upon such terms and in such manner as the board of directors may, from time to time, deem expedient or advisable, or to become a shareholder in any such corporation.
Now, I have read the entire transcript of the evidence in the hearing before the board of transport commissioners some months ago in which the Bell Telephone Company was seeking some adjustment in its rates and capitalization and in which the Industrial Wire and Cable Company-which is located close to my riding-entered objections as in-tervenor. Many questions were asked during the hearing before the board concerning Bell Telephone Company's control of Northern Electric. The evidence, given under oath and available from the public record, indicates that the president, vice president and general counsel of the Bell Telephone Company

pointed out that they were able to buy the shares of Northern Electric Company because Northern Electric owned a telephone company. Thus, section 4 of their charter allowed them to own another telephone company.
Well, further evidence brought out the fact that there is a telephone line of 19,000 feet in length between the Northern Electric plant in Montreal and one building of the Bell Telephone Company. You and I, being laymen in this telephonic communication business, would think the telephone line owned exclusively by Northern Electric would be a telephone line that you could go out and see with the naked eye, a telephone line over which persons such as you and I could talk to one another. Far be it for me to expose the situation, but I should like to quote from the board of transport commissioners. It appears from the evidence that the value of Bell Telephone Company's shareholdings in Northern Electric was $34 million. They said at that time they owned 90 per cent of the stock, and it has since been increased. If they had a $34 million investment in Northern Electric Company when they appeared before the board of transport commissioners a year ago, by adding 10 per cent we are within reason in saying that they must have a $38 million investment in Northern Electric now.
I mentioned that increasing the number of directors from 15 to 20 is probably necessary in order for Bell Telephone to strengthen the bond between Bell and Northern, because some of these directors would be interlocking directors. This investment of $38 million that the Bell Telephone Company has in Northern Electric shows up in their full beauty the two most valuable strands of copper wire in the Dominion of Canada. The evidence before the board of transport commissioners was to the effect that the Bell Telephone Company installed a telephone line for Northern Electric many years ago. After a year or so Northern Electric bought the telephone line from the Bell Telephone and thus become the proprietor of a telephone line.
Now, the charter of the Bell Telephone Company permits the company to buy any company that operates a telephone system. The interesting thing in the evidence was that there were only two strands in the telephone communication system which the Northern Electric Company operates in Montreal. What is further interesting is the fact that these two strands of copper wire are embedded in a major cable.

speechtext:
Order. The hon. member was good enough at the outset of his remarks

to indicate that he intended to establish a connection or relationship between what he is saying now and the bill presently before the committee. At the beginning of his remarks I thought there was some relevancy in what he was saying, but it seems to me that at this point he is referring to the technical operation of a company and I wonder whether this can properly be considered as relevant to the clause before the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I believe the hon. member is familiar with the rule of the house which requires members to deliver an oral presentation and argument unsupported by exhibits. We know that in courts of law the putting forward of exhibits is acceptable because exhibits can be filed and examined. But there is no such provision in relation to debates in this house and I would ask the hon. member to refrain from using exhibits at this time.
Mr. Cov/an: I appreciate your remarks, Mr. Chairman. I would not have thought of bringing in an exhibit were it not for the fact that many flags were introduced a while ago; they appeared on the desks of members for a while and were then voluntarily removed. However, I do not need a material exhibit to make my point-that in the middle of a large cable running from Northern Electric to the Bell Telephone Company building there are two thin strands of copper wire. They are tagged at either end with little tags to say that these two strands belong to Northern Electric. This is in accordance with testimony presented before the board of transport commissioners.
Hon. members may think these are valuable wires-two strands representing an investment worth $38 million. This works out at the rate of $5 million a mile per strand, I believe- I have not figured it out on paper. But the interesting thing is that you cannot talk from one end of the wire to the other in conversation. The wire carries the voice in only one direction-from the Northern Electric plant to the Bell Telephone plant. This appears in the testimony produced before the board of transport commissioners. Of course it may be that Northern Electric only needs to use this line to ask the Bell Telephone Company what it must do next. Then I suppose the Bell Telephone Company either sends a mes-

Private Bills
senger across to tell them what to do next or calls Northern Electric over the Bell Telephone system. But the capital ownership of Northern Electric by Bell is based on section 4 of a statute which gives the Bell Telephone Company the right to own a company which owns a telephone line and, as I have explained, Northern Electric owns a telephone line 19,000 feet long consisting of two strands of copper wire within a larger cable.
A little while ago the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hahn) gave an illuminating address on the manner in which Canadian taxpaying companies engaged in the production of wires and telephone equipment are in open competition with the Northern Electric Company which does a $150 million a year business with the Bell Telephone Company. I might point out that the Bell Telephone Company, as a consequence of its compensatory advantages, was able to put in a tender to the C.B.C. 25 per cent lower than either the C.P.R. or the C.N.R. were able to offer after 30 years experience of operation. It is obvious that the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. should know what it costs to service 195 radio stations. But when the contract came up for tender two years ago the Bell Telephone Company was able to undercut the tenders submitted by both the railway companies. As the presidents of both of these vast organizations pointed out in a letter to the government of the day, it would be interesting to know if it is fair, in the communication business, that a competitor should be able to undercut tenders on a competitive basis while fattening its profits in unregulated fields.
There is a great deal of dissatisfaction at the present time at this arrangement by which the stock of the Northern Electric Company is 100 per cent held by the Bell Telephone Company. A hearing has been held before the board of transport commissioners and Mr. Venne, solicitor for the company, who appeared before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines mentioned that the board of transport commissioners had decided it was perfectly legal for the company to hold the stock. Mr. Chairman, the board of transport commissioners is not a court of law. Mr. Venne told the committee that the board was "a court of record-a court of law". But it is not; and Mr. P. C. Venne, Q.C., general counsel for the Bell Telephone Company, knows it better than we do. The board of transport commissioners is a regulatory body and, like other great empire builders in the vast reaches of government, it seeks perpetually to increase its empire. Under the IMr. Cowan.]
terms of the Railway Act which established the board of transport commissioners the board is authorized to make rules, regulations, orders and decisions. But it has come to the point where the board of transport commissioners when it renders a decision or makes an order places on top of it, the word "judgment". Mr. Chairman, they may think they are judges, but they are not judges and these are not legal rulings. The board of transport commissioners makes decisions or determinations.
I should like to suggest in the interest of the voters in my riding, in the interests of Industrial Wire and Cable and in the interests of millions of others in Canada that a request be made to the Supreme Court of Canada for a review to be made of the relationship between these two companies which are so closely knit together, one of them under so-called public regulation and the other under no regulation at all-the Bell Telephone Company and Northern Electric. Is this a combine in restraint of trade? Is this arrangement in violation of the restrictive trade practices act? Many people are asking these questions.
We were told during the sittings of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, that the total income of the Bell Telephone Company in 1962 amounted to $471 million. What amazed us was to hear-and I think this information was given to us somewhat unintentionally-that the company paid the American Telephone and Telegraph Corporation of the United States 1 per cent of its income every year for research. I put a specific question to the officers of the Bell Telephone Company. I asked whether they meant 1 per cent of the gross income or of the net income. And they said it was 1 per cent of the gross. Now, on a gross income of $471 million in 1962, 1 per cent comes to $4,710,000 a year. I think it was the hon. member for Villeneuve, speaking some weeks ago on this bill, who asked whether income tax was being paid to the Canadian government on all the moneys earned by Bell Telephone. It would be interesting to know whether any tax is paid on this $4,710,000 which is sent to the United States under the guise of funds for research. We were told there were 15,000 employees in the research department of the A. T. and T. and that the Bell Telephone Company of Canada has the right to draw on all the results of the studies made by these ladies and gentlemen in the United States. I wonder whether the Department of National Revenue checks to find out whether the A. T. and T. in fact spends $4,710,000 on research work

for the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. Perhaps they only spend $500,000 for research for the Bell Telephone Company. I would not know, never having been given an opportunity of looking into the books in that way. It is interesting in connection with that $4,710,000, that the Bell Telephone Company has a director representing the A.T.T. from the States, and we are pretty certain where the company is controlled despite all the wide publicity about 207,000 shareholders resident in Canada.
They told us in the committee meeting that maybe 300 people attend the annual meeting, and of course the voting is controlled by proxies; but it would be interesting to know what research the A.T.T. is going to do in the United States in connection with the false siren alarm that went off in Ottawa last Saturday. This siren system is operated by the Bell Telephone Company, and with all this money going to research one would have thought they would have found a way of overcoming shotgun pellets setting a city of 300,000 people on its ear, just because somebody was shooting starlings sitting on a telephone wire.
Are we getting value for the money we allow the Bell Telephone Company to send out of Canada for research in the United States on behalf of a Canadian company? We talk about the brain drain to the United States and about how there are few opportunities for our educated young men and women in Canada to engage in research. Why in the name of heaven can't this money be held back in Canada and research conducted in this dominion, or are they taking Canadians down into the United States to conduct research on money earned in Canada and shipped down to the United States, and no doubt classified as an expense to the company?
I am speaking on behalf of a fine company, Industrial Wire and Cable, which is engaged in a very competitive business. The hon. member for Broadview showed that a couple of weeks ago, and I believe it is entitled to every protection the government and the law can afford it. I do not think it should be forced to compete on an open market with a company subsidized to the extent of $150,000,000 a year in equipment purchases by the Bell Telephone Company, which does not go on the open market and ask for competitive prices.
I would suggest, before I make way for some other valuable contributions on this subject-because I know some are going to be made-the air will not be cleared until
Private Bills
there has been an open reference to the Supreme Court of Canada for an investigation into the method of control of the Northern Electric Company by the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. When Industrial Wire and Cable tried to appeal the decision of the board of transport commissioners to the Supreme Court of Canada, they got a curt refusal, that as their application involved a mixture of law and fact the supreme court would not be able to review it. If Industrial Wire and Cable are not given the opportunity of paying for an appeal to the supreme court, then I say the government of the day should see that such a reference is made. A final decision must be made on this matter of interest to millions of Canadians, a matter that has interested them for many years and will continue to interest them until a final decision is made by the most competent of authorities, and not such a board as the board of transport commissioners.

Mr. Chairman, I have followed with great interest the speeches made in this debate today, and I am particularly interested in the reasons and the suppositions put forward for an increase in the number of directors of this company. On behalf of several members of my party, as well as for myself I would like to thank the mover of this bill for the courtesy he paid us in introducing us to a vice president of the Bell Telephone Company and discussing with us some of the problems we raised. Following that meeting the vice president of the company wrote me a letter saying that although he could not agree with all the matters raised he was pleased that the conversation remained on a friendly and cordial basis. That is true, but we are not really interested in the cordial and friendly basis. We are interested in the reasons for the increase in number of the board of directors.
The relationship between the Bell Telephone Company and the Northern Electric Company has created a great deal of controversy in the minds of many hon. members, especially the method used in acquiring Northern Electric Company. Many hon. members have asked questions about this, which the board of transport commissioners will have to answer. It is not quite correct, in my opinion, for the mover of the bill to say that the matter about the ownership of Northern Electric and the interalliance between the two companies could be raised by Industrial Wire and Cable whenever that company wished it to be raised. As I remember

Private Bills
it, this matter was asked to be deferred by the board itself, and the second part of the inquiry was left in abeyance and remains in abeyance. It would appear that because of this request there will have to be a further request from Industrial Wire and Cable before the matter is brought before the public once more.
I make no apology for saying my interest in this is more on the subscribers' side than the Northern Electric side of the question, but I do endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands who said Bell Telephone Company is a monopoly company, that it operates in a monopolistic field, that this field has to be a monopoly, and that we representing the people of Canada must show some interest in the relation of the Bell Telephone Company to its subscribers and to the interests of the country.
The siren alarm which was mentioned by the hon. member for York-Humber gives rise to one of the problems that the board of transport commissioners will have much difficulty in settling. I believe the Bell Telephone Company is away out of its jurisdiction in many fields in which it operates, and it is for this reason we think part of the board of directors must represent the public of Canada.
I was very pleased to hear the vice president of the company tell us that he expected at least one or two of the proposed new directors would be appointed from the university level, that they would be academic people chosen to give the board a broader public representation than it now has, but I discount his suggestion that this is to allow the vice presidents to take turns in going on the board of directors. I do not believe that is correct; I do not believe that is necessary, and I do not believe it would serve the interests of the company, of the subscribers, and more particularly of the shareholders to have additional directors appointed from the management side of the company.
I am sure the management and the board of directors have discussed this with each other. I am sure they are willing to allow the vice presidents to appear on the board of directors, with voice but without vote, and such nominees would appear in a managerial status.
I am interested in this matter because of the picture that is shown by the financial statements of the various companies held by Bell Telephone, and also because of the high rates charged to subscribers to the Bell Telephone system. An indication of this is the

Montreal system where the private rate is $6.46. In Ottawa it is $5.46, and in Halifax the Maritime Telephone Company rate is $5.35. In Saskatchewan the system is operated by a provincial telephone exchange under the government and there the rate is only $3.90. In Regina, under the Saskatchewan provincial government the rate is $3.90. This may double in the next few weeks owing to the change of government, but at the time I obtained these figures it was $3.90. The Alberta government system is $3.50.
I do not want to go into all the ramifications of these figures, Mr. Chairman, but let no hon. member confuse himself into believing that it is cheaper to operate a rural telephone system than an urban telephone system. But the Bell Telephone urban systems are almost double the cost to the subscriber of the rural telephone systems. This is the reason we wish to have some control and why I wish to move an amendment. This amendment, in my mind, will allow you and I and the people of Canada to give the Bell Telephone Company, in an academic sense, the chance to have certain people on their board of directors, so as to give it the allure they wish the board to present. I move:
That clause 1 of the bill be amended by striking out lines 9 to 21 thereof and substituting therefor the following:
"8. The business of the company shall be managed by a board of not less than five nor more than twenty directors, as may from time to time be determined by resolution of the shareholders, and three such directors shall be appointed by the governor in council and each other such director, additional to these three, shall be the proprietor of at least ten shares in the capital stock of the company, or such other additional number of shares, not exceeding forty additional shares, as the shareholders shall by any resolution passed at any annual general meeting, or special general meeting, from time to time determine; and the said board of directors, save as in this section provided, shall be elected and hold office as hereinafter provided; and all the directors so appointed shall be Canadians resident in Canada and a majority, where more than two, of the directors so elected shall be residents of Canada".
We have discussed this matter, Mr. Chairman, with the vice president of the company. As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands has pointed out, this gentleman said: "This is a very interesting idea but why pick on me? Why not pick on the Canadian Pacific Railway?" I suppose he chose the C.P.R. because it is larger than the Bell Telephone Company, is in the public domain and in a monopoly field as well. We believe that if what the sponsor has said is representative of the thinking of the majority of the board of directors who are asking parliament

to increase the number of directors, then we can supply what they seem to require and increase the board in a way which will give it the appearance of impartiality which I think the vice president indicated was desirable. This could be accomplished by letting the governor in council appoint three of the directors.
There are a number of ways of doing this. Originally I thought we should buy stock in the company; that perhaps the government should take it over as a crown corporation. However, I think this is a very mild way of exerting some authority which I think the board of transport commissioners has been unable to exert.
I sincerely believe that if we are wrong in our supposition that the Northern Electric Company is being used for ulterior purposes, if we are wrong in our belief that rural telephones are more expensive to operate than urban telephone exchanges, and if we are wrong in assuming that the rate in Ottawa should be lower than the rate in rural parts of Ontario and rural parts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the maritimes as well, then I believe that these representatives, the ombudsmen, really, of the federal government in this monopoly jurisdiction, will serve the Bell Telephone Company well. We certainly will not appoint low class people, but they will be ordinary people representative of the Canadian government who will act responsibly in representing the Bell Telephone, but who will act also to represent the people of Canada, the subscribers of the Bell Telephone Company and all other interested parties, including the competitors of this company in one of its fields.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before I close those brief remarks, I should like to point out to the minister, as I did this afternoon, that the government is often weak enough to yield to repeated requests from pressure groups which pretend to exercise the privileges of democracy, but which often represent but a very slight percentage of their alleged supporters.
By means of blatant publicity, with the help of newspapers, radio and television, and

Supply-Health and Welfare also as a result of polls conducted by people who handle election campaigns, such associations or pressure groups, who often represent only a very low percentage of the mass of private individuals who are supposed to be concerned, influence the government to such an extent that it will finally propose social legislation which, no matter how attractive it might be from a humanitarian viewpoint, proves disastrous from an economic and social point of view. Once again, I shall caution the minister against this excessive enthusiasm which could result from the application of a social measure. I feel that if the government spent more money for medical research on cancer, not only in connection with the use of tobacco but with regard to cancer itself, cardiovascular diseases and mental illness, it would render a much greater service to the people than if it decided to increase its contribution in the field of social security.
I should like to quote from memory the words of Mr. Claude Jourdain, former Liberal member for Gaspe North in the Quebec legislature. Speaking before the economic council of the Gaspe peninsula, he said that the government should reduce, if not abolish, all social security benefits, so that the people of his district-and I think this could be implemented on a national basis-would decide to earn their living by working instead of relying on state assistance. In addition, Mr. Jourdain said that such a measure would not increase the popularity of any political party but that, for the good of the citizens of his region, a political party just had to take a decision to that effect.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that the government should rather try to solve the unemployment problem, to abolish salary differentials in various regions, in short to help the Canadian citizens to earn their living by themselves instead of making them dependant on the state, because it is a well-known fact that everything that pertains to the state is much more costly than that which has nothing to do with it.
The minister also talked about a new organization set up by the Department of National Health and Welfare to deal with the marketing of new drugs.
At this stage, I should like to point out that the food and drugs committee did some most interesting work not because I was one of its members but because all the other members were most objective in the serious and precise questions they asked the representatives of various groups. In fact, I am sure


that the committee's recommendations will be advantageous not only to the department but to every Canadian.
I should also like to say a word about amateur sport. I suppose the hon. member who will speak after me-the name of his riding has slipped my mind for the moment- will also discuss that point since he has been interested in amateur sport for years.
Once again, I regret that the administration of amateur sports comes under the Department of National Health and Welfare. However, since this division of the department is still at the organization stage we have no choice but to go along with it. I believe that the country, in general, should do even more than it does at present for amateur sports.
There are several good reasons to change such a policy. First of all, we know that amateur sport will go a long way to give a good physical education to our young people, to improve the physical fitness of the whole population and especially, to bolster the reputation of Canada at the international level in the field of sports.
When we see, for instance, that hockey clubs representing Canada at the Olympic games or in world tournaments are generally second class clubs, except last year, when a new system was given a try, it is really humiliating for Canada to realize that while our country has a monopoly, if we may say so, in regard to the quality of hockey at home, it is being defeated by much inferior countries on the international level, merely because the government did not want to take its responsibilities in that regard and did not make a sufficient financial contribution to certain teams that could have been worthy representatives.
Be that as it may, it is a pleasure to note the continuous progress made in the Department of National Health and Welfare. We hope that the department will not fall into the same traps as other countries, which turned out to be economically disastrous.
We hope that from now on and little by little, the Minister of National Health and Welfare will heed the advice of the various groups represented in this house who reflect Canadian public opinion, so that the legislation to be introduced by the Department of National Health and Welfare and by other departments will really promote the welfare of the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I hope hon. members of the committee will permit me to interject something at this time while there

are a number of members present in the chamber.
Earlier this afternoon many hon. members joined me in extending felicitations to my departmental secretary. Since that time I have learned that today is a very special day in the life of my senior deputy, the deputy minister of health, who has held that office for nearly 20 years. Since 1926 he has taken over a number of new ministers, three at least, and led them, if not down the garden path, at least up the path through the administration.
Dr. Donald Cameron is a man much beloved by those associated with him, not only by ministers but by very many members of parliament who over the years have had occasion to seek his advice and assistance. Today is his 65th birthday. Normally that would be the signal for his retirement, but he has been good enough to agree to serve Canada for at least one additional year. I am happy that this year saw the opening of the new building and I am happy that I have this opportunity on behalf of the thousands of people who work in the department of health and who have known him over the years to offer my felicitations to him. I am also happy, Mr. Chairman, to provide an opportunity at the close either of today's sitting or of the estimates, whichever first occurs, when many of his friends will be able to come to my office and to give him greetings. In concluding, I should like to offer to him a token of our esteem, even if the Sergeant-at-Arms may have it removed shortly thereafter. I apologize to him because for all I know perhaps it should be a Tory blue cornflower, but I should like him to accept this red rose.

May I say that the hon. member for Perth and I have been associated with the deputy minister of health for a great number of years. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this time I should like to say a few words about the physical fitness program. As we all know, the physical fitness program of the Department of National Health and Welfare has been the subject of criticism under both governments and I am afraid that I have been one of the main critics, as has the hon. member for Peel. However, in addition to offering a few suggestions at this time which I think are vital to the success of a physical fitness program I should also like to give a few bouquets.
First I want to congratulate the minister on the increase in the funds allocated to Olympic teams. This in itself has automatically caused more interest not only within the different organizations receiving the funds but also among the Canadian people themselves. The very fact of receiving these grants has lent an added incentive to the teams and organizations concerned. We all know there are different groups within any Olympic organization. Some are able to raise funds because they are a group that appeals to the public and they can get people to come out to see them perform. Others cannot. These grants will add to their incentive to work to raise funds to send their representatives to the Olympics.
Our Prime Minister, who we have to admit is a really true sportsman and athlete in every sense of the word, is to be commended highly for taking time out of his very busy schedule to attend athletic functions such as the Canadian Henley at St. Catharines and the Olympic track and field trials at St. Lambert, Quebec. There is little doubt in the minds of all of us, I am sure, that his presence at these functions must have not only added prestige to them but have contributed to the morale of the athletes participating in the events.
It was also rather gratifying to have the Minister of National Health and Welfare attend the Olympic games at Innsbruck, representing the government of Canada. I would not say that I agreed with everything she said after she came back, but the fact is that Canada had a fine representative there. I do


not know whether this was the first time that Canada was represented at the Olympic games by such a person. At the Olympic games this fall in Tokyo the hon. member for York West, the one and only Red Kelly, is going to represent the Canadian government. As we all know, he is one of the most respected and outstanding young athletes today and I am sure all members will agree that Canada will be well and truly represented by him.
I would be very remiss indeed if I did not mention the wonderful Father Bauer at this time. Surely Canada must be very proud, not only of his work as a coach of our Olympic team but of the great respect he brought to himself, to his team and to the people of Canada as a result of the true sportsmanship shown by him during the hockey championships. Those were very trying circumstances, and Canada can be proud of the fact we had such a wonderful young gentleman handling our team.
I mentioned previously a little bit about grants. I just want to say this, that as important as grants are to our teams and to our athletic organizations, the most important feature by far-let us get this straight now- of any physical fitness program is the child, our youth in the country. Naturally, any physical fitness program that deals with children has to start in the school itself. I realize that schools mean education and education is a provincial matter. However I sincerely hope that perhaps as a result of the co-operation of the provinces we may be able to put a federal program into the schools right across Canada.
There is one thing however that we can do federally to get this physical fitness program off the ground. This is something that is absolutely necessary if any physical fitness program is to succeed. I refer to the need for facilities. If we have not got facilities, nothing can happen. Today, more than any time in our history, we need these facilities. We are living in an age entirely different from the past. Our boys and girls go to school in buses or drive their own cars. We are living in a different age under different conditions. We do need a physical fitness program more than ever. There are many areas in the different parts of Canada that are practically devoid of facilities, track and field, arenas, swimming pools and so forth.
The reference to swimming pools reminds me of a situation in the minister's constituency. I do not know whether or not she realizes it, but there is only one covered

swimming pool in the Niagara district to take care of something like 60,000 people. I am going to say this, that in West Germany, a country that was devastated during the war, they have a program which covers 15 years and is called the "golden plan". This program will provide a billion and a half dollars worth of facilities for the youth of that country. So we can go ahead and take this $5 million grant which, so far as I am concerned, is slowly being used up. This is merely a pittance to a country like Canada that has not felt the ravages of war. We could start off with $15 million or $25 million and it would be money well spent. Let me tell you that money spent on sports will return more than dollars and cents to the people and the communities of this nation. It will make returns in the form of good citizenship, and God only knows we need it these days.
I have just finished reading quite an interesting little book entitled "Soviet and Sport", by Dr. Henry W. Morton a member of the faculty of Queen's University. I have no intention of dealing with these matters because they would take up all my time; however, I should like to point out something. The U.S.S.R. has a seven year plan which will be completed in 1967. Do you know what is going to happen by that time? One out of every four people, a quarter of the population of the U.S.S.R., will belong to a sports organization. Remember, this quarter of the people of Russia will be the vital, youthful sector of that society, and that really means something. The Soviets do not look upon sport as a means for creating only physical fitness, health and stamina. They look upon it also as a means of ensuring the prestige of their country in the world today, in the sport world. Whether we like it or whether we do not, during peacetime we need this and our young people need it. They need sport; they need relaxation to burn up their energies. We are having enough trouble as it is and one reason for that is that we are not properly organized for sport activities in which the young people can take part.
I do not know whether you realize the important part our young athletes really play in bringing respect to Canada and Canadians throughout the world today. I do not know whether you realize it or not but you can be in Canada today and in Europe tomorrow. It was not always this way. Our soldiers were recognized in the first and second world wars; they really let the world know what Canada was. What about the big space between the two world wars? What about the big space
Supply-Health and Welfare following the last war? Tourists were not going over there then because they did not have the money they have today. There were a few members of the government and businessmen going over at that time, but how did Canada become the respected nation she is today? How did that old maple leaf become what it is and how was it kept in front of the people? I will tell you. Mr. Frank Sargent, past president of the Canadian amateur hockey association took a team on tour through Europe at that time. They went over by boat and spent some time in the countries of Europe. This is what the top government men, the top men in the cities and communities in which they played hockey said-just try and get this because I have never forgotten it: Outside of war, the only time we ever hear the name "Canada" mentioned is when your young athletes tour our country with their hockey teams and play their games in our cities.
I am going to say this, that sport is the greatest means for breaking down barriers; it is the common denominator that creates equality. It does not make any difference whether you are red or yellow or black; it does not make any difference whether you are Catholic, Jewish or Protestant, in these sport lanes you are as one. Let us never forget that. It does do something else, it makes you value one another. The value of sport cannot be added up in dollars and cents. I just want to bring one further thought to you about the Soviet union and sport. This is the most important thing so far as the U.S.S.R. is concerned, that sport organizations are used as the means of rallying the working men around the various party government and training organizations, and are automatically drawn into the social and political life of the nation. That is why they are doing it. That is why they have a quarter of their youth tied up in sports organizations. I will not go as far as to say the same should be done in Canada. But I do believe that physical fitness and sport should and could play a far greater role in the life of our nation.
