I should like to add my personal congratulations and felicitations to Dr. Cameron on his sixty fifth anniversary. I should also like to add my personal suggestion to him, that in view of his fitness physically as well as mentally he should continue to offer his services to his country in some way and not allow the fact that he has reached this milestone to persuade him to retire to some position where he could not do anything either for himself or for his country
7856	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare and where his qualities would deteriorate. I feel men of his experience are so valuable to their country that they should not allow such milestones as these to interfere with their future activities for our welfare.
I am happy to have this opportunity to make a few observations with regard to this important and interesting department. The department of health and welfare is probably the most important of all the departments of the federal government. Now that it has reached a wonderful position of being able to spend more than $2 billion annually, I think it is in the top bracket of all the government departments. As far as the estimates before us are concerned, I have no particular objection to the items which are included, or to the remarks which have been made by the minister. My complaint is directed, rather, to the omissions.
I do not wish to delay passage of these estimates unduly. Indeed I think they should be passed without much delay. I spoke in November of last year on the estimates of this department and at that time I stressed the great importance of medical research. This evening I wish to continue in that vein. I feel this is probably the most important field which lies before the department today. Indeed it is probably the most important question facing medical science in Canada today and I believe it offers an opportunity for the government to provide assistance so as not only to save money for the taxpayer but also to improve our scientific status as a nation. There have been suggestions that further grants will be made, and I am grateful for them. But I feel these improvements are only fractional. I believe, and I am sure the vast majority of the medical profession in Canada would agree with me, that as far as the government is concerned medical research is a neglected child in Canada. As I have already mentioned, this is a most vital need if medical science is to advance; it is vital, also, to the educational services of medicine.
I had hoped to speak on this subject when the estimates of the research council were before the committee for consideration, but unfortunately there was no opportunity to do so. I should like to suggest now that the subject of the research council is closely allied with the observations I am making this evening. The council has added to its budget the sum or $1.8 million. There is no question but that we are grateful for this addition. But I would draw this to the attention of the committee: $1.8 million is just the equivalent of the grants received from the United States


which are being cancelled. So we are just where we began before this grant was made; there has really been no increase. Canada today needs to double this amount in order to be effective in this great field of medical research. I should like to suggest three pertinent questions to this committee. I should like to ask why Canadians in the upper income bracket frequently find it advisable to go to the United States institutions for medical treatment. I do not endorse this practice; I feel it is unnecessary. But it is a fact that it exists. I would even get down to a more personal question and ask why it is that members of this House of Commons go to the United States for medical care. It is unnecessary. We can do the same things here in Canada. But this is the situation which exists today. What happens when people go to the United States? In many cases they are treated by Canadians, men who trained at Canadian universities, graduated there and went to the United States to work. It reminds one of the well known story of the Scotsman who made his first business trip to London. When he returned to Glasgow they asked him how he got along with Englishmen, and he replied: Englishmen? I didn't see any Englishmen. I only talked with heads of firms.
Let me repeat, there are approximately 350 Canadian medical men who go to take up practice in the United States every year. They are replaced by about 100 who come here from Europe, so we have a deficit of 250 every year. These doctors go to the United States partly because of the climate and partly because of economic reasons. But I am glad to say that medical men in general are not influenced in going to the United States for economic reasons. They go there mostly because of the scientific advantages, and that is why we are experiencing this terrible drain of graduates from Canadian universities. We are spending money on training these people but they go to the United States where they are offered better facilities and very few of them ever return to Canada.
I should like to put on the record a report from New York which was published in the Toronto Globe and Mail on August 4 of this year under the name of Frederick Hodgson, and these are the views of Canadian scientists attending the sixth international congress of biochemistry. I will not detain the committee by putting the whole report on record, but this paragraph is of particular interest because it has a direct bearing on the subject I am dealing with tonight. This is what it says:

Unless Ottawa loosens the federal purse strings and pours more millions into basic scientific research, particularly into the biological and medical fields, there will be a mass migration of Canadian scientists to laboratories and universities in the United States.
I should like to quote now from Dr. John T. Edsall, head of the department of biochemistry at Harvard University, who backed up this prediction by saying:
This is not a brain drain engineered by the United States. It is an insane export of scientific manpower. If I can't get support for my work in my own country then I've got to go where I can get that support.
Canada is rich enough to stand on her own two feet scientifically.
He continued in the same vein:
Grants to research laboratories in Canada have been cut by about 20 per cent this year-
These are the American grants he is speaking of.
-with an additional cut of 40 per cent due in the next fiscal year.
He continued at great length, but I shall only burden you with one more quotation, in which he said he saw no other way to give Canada scientific independence than to get Canada to contribute more to scientific research. That is what we are facing in Canada today.
I also have here the report of the National Research Council of Canada for 1962-63. This year's report is not out yet, but here are a couple of sentences from the report of the vice president, Dr. R. F. Farquharson, who is well known to many hon. members:
Two great shortages currently exist in Canada's medical research program. One of these is the small number of full time appointments in Canadian medical schools, particularly in clinical departments. Because of its heavy teaching load, the small full time staff has inadequate time for research.
Further on he made this statement:
The other great shortage is of research laboratories. In all our universities there is a serious lack of space for the work that must be done. This shortage is becoming a critical factor actively interfering with further progress. It also aggravates the tendency for good people to seek positions outside the country.
This is a serious situation and I do not think we in the House of Commons are aware of the seriousness of it. Economically it is to our advantage to pay some attention to this matter. We have more medical schools than are actually necessary in Canada today, if we could keep our doctors at home. At the present time, without allowing for increased population, if we could keep our medical graduates at home we would not need any
Supply-Health and Welfare more medical schools. We have 12 of them but we lose 30 per cent of their graduates to the United States.
When health insurance is introduced there will be a greater demand than ever for medical graduates, and I know we will need more medical schools because of increased population but, as I say, we have enough now if we could keep the graduates in Canada. We would save ourselves the extra expense of more schools if we could keep our people from migrating, and the unfortunate thing is that in this migration we are losing our scientific leaders and many of our potential teachers. We are losing the individuals with inquiring minds, and they are leaving because of exasperation and frustration. They are leaving because of lack of facilities to carry on the work they want to do in Canada, and they are finding greater opportunities to develop their research tendencies in other countries.
I have another short quotation here, this one from Sir Howard Florey, delivering his David Rivett memorial lecture at the University of Melbourne:
There are, of course, personal rivalries between laboratories, between universities and between countries, but the desire to know, and the desire to know first, explains a great deal of the drive of scientists for ever better facilities and their increasing tendency to go to whatever country is prepared to offer them a satisfactory scientific life.
This is what is happening to Canada. Canada has reached a crisis in regard to its medical education. The time was when Canada led the world but today we are becoming a second or third rate medical country. The teachers with the exploring minds are going elsewhere. They go where they can get the top medical research facilities.
In the amount of money we devote for scientific research in medicine, how do we compare with the sums provided in other countries? Per capita and on a gross national basis for every $1 donated in the United States toward medical research Britain donates 20 cents and Canada 15 cents, and that 15 cents includes what we get from philanthropic sources. We cannot look with any pride on the fact that we donate only 15 cents per head as compared with $1 per head in the United States.
As a country we should realize that if we are to hold our place in the world we must donate what is relatively fair in proportion to our gross national product. The United States donates more than six times as much as we do in Canada, and therefore it is obvious

Supply-Health and Welfare why Canadians will go to the United States for medical care. It is also obvious why our best scientists go to the United States, and it is obvious why our medical schools are tending to deteriorate.
Unfortunately those of our doctors who stay in Canada have to teach yesterday's medicine, and yesterday's medicine is not good enough for today, and it will be worse for tomorrow. We are simply failing to keep pace with world development. As I have said, our medical schools are becoming second and third rate. At one time, not many generations ago, they were the best medical schools in the world but now they are gradually deteriorating. We must do something about it, and we must do it now.
I congratulate the minister upon her announcement the other day of a fine contribution towards the extension of the medical research facilities in the University of British Columbia. I happen to be familiar with that undertaking, as I come from B.C. myself, and I congratulate the minister on the assistance being offered to Dr. J. McCreary, dean of medicine there. He is undertaking a wonderful experiment, and I understand she is also assisting medical education in other provinces. This is something which should be extended across the nation.
The Farquharson report, which was the result of an investigation of the situation not long ago, indicated we required not only grants for the salaries and for the upkeep of these institutions but that $37 million was required to construct proper facilities for research centres in hospitals and universities. That report, as I recall it, came in about two years ago, although I may be out a year or so. But the fact is that what was going to cost $37 million at that time will now cost $60 million, and the longer we put it off the greater will be the cost.
There is also a large amount of expenditure on the part of drug and pharmaceutical firms in Canada as well as their associated organizations in the United States. As a member of the committee of this house on food and drugs it was my privilege to visit some of the research laboratories in Canada, and I feel that we should all be appreciative of the work which these people are doing. They are doing fine work as far as research is concerned, and I think that if it is necessary for us to assist them in some way we should be prepared to do so. But we should under any circumstances be prepared to increase the amount of grants we are presently making

to these objects. It is extremely important that we do so.
On a recent trip to Montreal the members of the food and drugs committee were allowed the privilege of visiting several laboratories. In this connection I should like to draw to the attention of this committee an article which happened to be on my desk this dinner recess, having come in in today's mail. I think it is rather interesting. It refers to a Dr. Hans Selye, a man of whom we in Canada should be very proud. He is doing wonderful work and is so engrossed in scientific research that no amount of money would influence him to go anywhere else. Part of this article reads as follows:
In the face of strong opposition, Selye devoted himself to the task of finding the causes of this stress syndrome and, in moments of doubt, he gained added strength from the fact that one of the most noted Canadian scientists, Sir Frederick Banting, has been interested in his studies from the outset. As an adviser for the national research council, a government body, Banting visited university laboratories throughout the country and, when he came to Montreal, he often dropped into Selye's small, crammed laboratory and listened attentively to the young research worker. Banting was also responsible for Selye's first financial support, a modest grant of $500.
"But this was not as important to me as the moral support and encouragement I derived from being taken seriously by the discoverer of insulin," Dr. Selye recalls. He continued his investigations and perseverance brought success.
Also while in Montreal we had the opportunity to visit the laboratory of Dr. Genest in the Hotel Dieu, who is doing probably some of the world's greatest research into cardiovascular disease, particularly in regard to arteriosclerosis and high blood pressure. I am sure that everyone in the house should have the opportunity to visit his laboratory, because I never saw anything so disgraceful in my life. This gentleman is doing national work. His office is so crowded with books and diplomas that he hardly has a place to sit down, and his laboratory is equally overcrowded. He has visitors from all the large institutions in the United States, where they have all the facilities to work with, and who come to him because he is doing wonderful work under these adverse circumstances.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that we have to wake up and increase our grants toward medical research or we are not only going to lose our status in the medical world but also our scientists will be lost to the United States and things will get worse. We can save ourselves money if we take an interest in this subject and in those engaged on medical re-

search in our country. In this way we can re-establish ourselves to the position which is ours. I say that today we are in a period of explosive scientific development. Do you realize, Mr. Chairman, that 90 per cent of all the scientists who ever lived in the world are alive today? That is a very striking statement but I have that on very good authority. Scientific developments and knowledge are increasing so rapidly that they are going ahead at lightning speed, and wealthy countries like Canada-and we are a wealthy country-must develop our scientific resources or we are going to lose them. We have everything here to work with. I say let us save our scientists for Canada. Let us save our prestige in the field of medicine. Let us save our medical schools and develop and maintain adequate research facilities. Let us pay adequate salaries to those willing to dedicate their lives to medical research in the interests of the welfare of human beings, and let us wake up to our urgent responsibilities. I ask the government to act now because tomorrow may be too late. In the interests of science and national economy let us extend our medical research facilities so as to preserve not only our scientists but also probably postpone the immediate necessity for building more medical schools.

Mr. Chairman, I want to associate myself with the minister and others in congratulating the deputy minister. I might say that Welland had an earlier attraction for him as he came often in his earlier days, and won the hand of his better half, who is a very fine lady.
I want to say a few words tonight about the necessity for an increased grant to the health league of Canada. The health league of Canada has served the country for 45 years or more and as far as I know it was the only organization of that type in Canada. Other organizations have been formed since, but they have been segmentations of public spirited individuals who have joined together into associations, groups and the like, and devoted their work to a more specific aspect of health.
There are many things one could say about the health league of Canada. I think it is the only voluntary organization devoted mainly to the prevention of disease rather than to its cure. It is the only voluntary health organization in Canada with a charter which is concerned with an all-embracing interest in personal and community health. It is also the only organization in Canada with ex-
Supply-Health and Welfare perience in established policies and it is prepared to advance, either singly or in cooperation with other health agencies, the promotion of any new and improved health technique, thereby helping to improve the health of our people. I would suggest that the health league of Canada stands as a sentry in our society in respect of anything that may become a challenge to the best health treatment we can give. I can give one example of this fact. In my home town a few years ago the local anti-fluoridationists combined to have fluorine eliminated from our water supply. A vote was held and it was retained. The health league gave a great deal of assistance in this fight by supplying data, material and a great deal of other help. We preserved the practice of adding fluorine to our water, and this has certainly been beneficial to the condition of our children's teeth, and will continue to be so in the future.
Dr. Gordon Bates, head of the health league of Canada was the one man in the forefront promoting pasteurization of milk in Canada, as a result of which I am sure many lives have been saved. Dr. Bates was also in the forefront promoting the immunization of our citizens, although I know that many others were involved. The health league has done a great deal in promoting fluoridation of communal water supplies through the publication of its magazine and in other ways. I read an article about ten days ago in a Toronto newspaper which quoted a dentist as saying that the savings to the people in the city of Toronto alone as a result of fluoridation will in the future be as high as $1,200,000 per annum.
Mr. Chairman, grants from the federal government to the health league of Canada were at one time $25,000, although this has now been cut to $15,000. Since the period of that reduction the expenses of the health league have doubled as a result of increased postage charges on periodicals, which the league distributes, as well as the cost of raw materials and printing.
The voluntary health committee of the Senate and the House of Commons has received a great deal of co-operation from the health league of Canada as a result of the provision of speakers here at luncheon meetings, many of whom a great number of the members of this house have heard. I am sure we have all learned a great deal about the health league. The hon. member for Simcoe East was chairman of that health committee under the previous government, and I have

Supply-Health and Welfare filled that position during the last year or so. Our meetings have been held often and I am sure the members of that committee realize that with the increased need of assistance, the federal government grants to this health league are not sufficient. During successive years this committee has passed resolutions, which have been presented both to the previous minister of national health and welfare, and to the present minister, suggesting that this annual grant should be increased. I appeal to the present minister, who always has a keen sense in respect of the need to increase general health in our country, to give favourable consideration to the requests to increase this annual grant.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I should like to rise during what is left of this doctors' night in the House of Commons and make a few remarks. Before I do I should like to explain the exuberance of our party during the last few minutes. In the last few minutes we have learned that Mr. Renwick has just been conceded as the winner in the by-election in the Toronto Riverdale riding.
At this time, if there was no mention of the Hall commission report, I think we would be remiss. With all the medical-social recommendations that it contains, a person in my position is forced to endorse this report and advocate its full acceptance without, I hope, its being torn to shreds when it is produced as legislation in the house. The recommendations, including medical education and research facilities, relate to some of the most important needs of the present day. However, tonight I am not dealing with this subject, but rather I am going to discuss one of Canada's significant minority groups-that of the mentally retarded.
I appreciate the fact that the minister in her opening remarks mentioned the work the government is doing in this regard, but I consider it of sufficient importance to emphasize certain points. In Canada today there are more than 540,000 retarded persons, representing some 3 per cent of the population. Another 6.7 per cent of the population may be described as borderline. Of our retarded people, 116,000 are between the ages of 3 and 19.
Retarded persons may be divided into three classes. The first group comprises the 4 per cent who will never exceed the mental age of 4, and will always be dependant. The next group includes the 13 per cent who may achieve a mental age of 8, and can be trained to be partially self-sustaining. The largest group is the 83 per cent who may reach a

mental age of 12, and can be educated to be totally self-supporting. Of the 116,000 mentally retarded children in Canada, 96 per cent, or 111,000, are trainable. Yet only about 10 per cent of them are presently receiving training.
Dr. Donald Zarfas of the children's psychiatric research institute in London has said that prevention of retardation involves "prevention of deterioration in the retardate by helping him to overcome his handicaps as much as possible by good training programs." Education of the retarded is an expensive proposition. The cost of full time schooling is 400 to 600 per cent higher than for normal children, because of the special equipment, facilities and time required. It is estimated that day schools for 95,000 pupils, and boarding schools for another 10,000 are now needed. We must also provide for some 31,000 school-age children from rural areas. The cost of such a program, properly executed, could come to many millions of dollars, but surely we are practising false economy if we fail to spend this money.
Of those retardates who receive training, 83 per cent can be expected to support themselves, and another 13 per cent to support themselves to some extent. Ideally, only 4 per cent of the mentally retarded should be fully dependant.
In failing to provide adequate training, we fail to equip the retarded to support themselves, and thus render them dependant on public or private funds. The cost of supporting a dependant person through his lifetime is far in excess of the cost of the education that could and should be provided for him. Officials of the Canadian association of social workers state that retardation, in children and adults, forms one of their major problems in welfare work.
Beyond education itself, many other services must be provided. Diagnostic services are all important, so that mental retardation can be detected early and proper treatment instituted.
Home visiting services, vocational training, job placement services and recreational facilities are needed. Institutions for those who cannot live in the community are essential. At present some 18,000 persons are accommodated in 13 government supported institutions, all overcrowded. Another 19,000 retarded persons are in mental institutions; a highly unsatisfactory situation.
In order to carry out all these essential steps, more doctors, psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, nurses, occupational therapists and educationists are needed, and

provision must be made for their training. Canada's objectives should be those of the World Health Organization, expressed as follows:
All children irrespective of whether or not they suffer from mental or physical handicap, should have every access to the best medical diagnosis and treatment, allied therapeutic services, nursing and social services, education, vocational preparation, and employment. They should be able to satisfy fully the needs of their own personalities and become, as far as possible, independent and useful members of the community.
Beyond the problem of care is the problem of research in prevention of retardation. Here again, money spent now will mean a public saving in future years. To quote the World Health Organization again:
Every child has the right to expect the greatest possible protection against the occurrence of preventable physical or mental handicap before, during and after birth.
To date research has uncovered more than 100 causes of mental retardation. Other projects are under way to determine the early manifestations of retardation so that preventive measures or treatment may begin early. Psychological research is investigating the personality disorders that frequently accompany retardation, and research into the best methods of training and treatment is being conducted. In her maiden speech the hon. member for Saskatoon suggested research into sheltered employment situations for the mentally ill and such research should also be pursued for the retarded. This research is going on under the severe handicap of lack of funds. We must provide for an intensified research program if we expect to diminish the problem of the retarded.
The Hall commission report has included among its first priorities the recommendation that services to retarded children be made available under the mental health services and the health grant programs. I would most strongly urge that the government approach the October federal-provincial conference on retardation with these recommendations in mind. We can no longer afford to ignore the problem of the retarded. I should like to conclude my remarks by reading a short quotation:
Each of us is made up of the same 98 cents worth of chemistry, give or take a few cents depending upon inflation. The difference lies in abilities, not in feelings. Our retarded children have the same feelings of joy, sorrow, pain and fear as others and a few more of frustration. Comprehension is slower but they still want to be included and treated just as their more fortunate sisters, brothers and friends are treated.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this stage of the business of the house, I would be remiss if I did not stand up for the family, for its welfare, its needs and those of every individual.
The right to live is a strictly personal one. Life belongs to a person. The human person alone lives and has needs connected with the reality of life-every day, every month, and throughout the year. All the needs of each human being, whether they be material, spiritual or intellectual, may, in the present order of things, be met by means of one and the same instrument called money, or currency.
The inevitable conclusion is that this vital right is connected with the individual, and must follow the individual, if he is capable to administer his own life, or be paid to the head of the family or the institution responsible for that individual, if he is a dependant. The vital right, even in this case, remains a personal one, connected with the human person.
We also must inevitably conclude that, in a country of 19,200,000 people, there are necessarily 19,200,000 rights to live, ensuring to each human being a certain amount of money or currency to procure the goods or services strictly necessary to enable him to live- whether material, intellectual or spiritual.
And we come to another irrefutable conclusion:	that vital right is natural and
anterior to, or independent from, the capacity for work of each person, for its urgency applies in the same way to children, old and handicapped people, to the invalids, the sick, the blind, the students, the widows and mothers of families who are unable to work outside to earn their living, because it is their responsibility to work at home, and look after their children-their students or any other adult dependants.
The inevitable conclusion is that vital personal right, which at first sight seems to be of social, personal and family interest, becomes of national interest as soon as it has to be paid for in money, in cash-because only the national government of Canada holds the supreme authority on everything that has to do with money, its administration, its issuing, its circulation, its distribution to 19,200,000 human beings, in 4,700,000 families with children or dependants and to all the legal institutions, private or public, which have received from the governments administration charters. Only human beings exist, have the right to live; only human beings have life

Supply-Health and Welfare and the right to existence before all institutions, even before families.
Families and institutions are groups of men constituted by nature or society to facilitate the material, intellectual and spiritual life of human beings. Only men have the right to live and are entitled to the necessities of life and to the amount of money with which they can each day, each week, each month and each year, purchase the goods and services which are vital for their survival.
In my opinion, all those who hear this simple speech and all those who will read it will have to accept that unavoidable conclusion within the framework of our present system of government. Thus, the right to live is a matter which concerns the individual, the family, society and the nation.
Society is based on the person, and the person is the unit element of society. The family is already an institution, the first institution, the closest to the human being, the most responsible for the human being, from conception, birth, during infancy, adolescence, youth and even during middle age-for the weak, the sick or the cripple. If the family is first responsible for the human being, this responsibility is unavoidably exercised within organized society-and in this organization of the society, everything concerning money and its circulation is under the sole control of the Canadian government at Ottawa.
The inevitable conclusion is that the Canadian government at Ottawa is responsible for the vital rights of the individual within the boundaries of Canada, because only the Canadian government has full control and full authority over the whole monetary, economic and political machinery within the boundaries of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I think a few words should be said here about the importance of family allowances in our national economy, especially as an important part of the purchasing power of families. In keeping with the axiom "equal work, equal pay", it happens that both the single man and the family head get the same salary for the same work, that is, the same purchasing power. Now, inasmuch as he has a wife and children, the expenses of the head of a family are higher and require more purchasing power than those of a bachelor.
Governments have already thought of compensating for that difference by providing for income tax exemptions and certain family allowances, which simply proves that we are merely asking for corrections and adjustments in the figures laid down in the existing legislation, in order to make such legislation more

efficient, in keeping with the spirit which prevailed when it was discussed and passed.
The following table will show without the shadow of a doubt that this problem exists and that it must be solved immediately for the greater benefit of the whole national economy.
Today the number of workers has reached seven million people, half of whom are unmarried or married people without children. We see on one side:
3.500.000	fathers
3.500.000	mothers
7.000.	000 children
1.000.	000 students
15,000,000 consumers And on the other:
3,500,000	unmarried people
3,500,000	consumers
As the average salary is approximately $4,200 a year, we see on one side 15 million consumers living off the salary of 3,500,000 heads of family, and on the other, 3,500,000 consumers living off the salary of 3,500,000 unmarried or married people without children when the two spouses are in a position to work to earn a salary, such being the case with 80 per cent of young couples and even of couples who have brought up their families.
To show to what extent income tax exemptions and family allowances are inadequate to compare the family budget with that of the single person, one has only to examine the specific case of the head of an average family of five persons including three children earning all together average wages of $80 per week, that is $4,200 per year. How much more money will family allowances and the difference in income tax bring to the head of that family than to the single person who also earns $4,200?
A single person who earns $4,200 pays $458 in income tax after claiming his $1,000 exemption. Net income: $3,742. The head of a family who earns $4,200 pays $117 in income tax, after claiming his $2,000 exemption for himself and his wife and his $1,150 exemption for his three children, a 19 year-old student, a 14 year-old and an eight year-old. The 14 year-old child receives an allowance of $8 per month or $96 per year; the eight year-old child receives an allowance of $6 per month, or $72 per year. When this amount is added to the income we get $4,368 in

wages and allowances. $4,368 less $117 income tax leaves a net income of $4,251.
The net income of a father of three children, 19, 14 and eight years old, is $4,251, after he has paid $117 in income tax, whereas a bachelor who also earns $4,200 has a net income of $3,742, after he has paid $458 in income tax.
The difference in income tax and allowances gives to this head of family a net surplus of $509 to support his wife and his three dependant children. He gets $509 more for four more persons. That is $127.25 per annum for each person, or about $10.60 a month.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the naked truth. That is what the Minister of Finance believes to be the expression of economic justice between the people of this country.
Such is, Mr. Chairman and hon. members, what we are tolerating, what is taking place under our responsibility, our supreme monetary, economical and political authority in our parliament as well as in our national life. I would much rather have concealed those details instead of publishing them, so as to avoid the humiliation which is ours for having tolerated such an unfair situation for so long, for having delayed so long the small adjustment that has been necessary in our family allowances since their establishment in 1944, so as to restore a proper balance among the citizens who are assuming greater family responsibilities for the benefit of this country.
What are we going to do, Mr. Chairman, faced with these hard facts, with the sufferings and distress of our courageous heads of families who are never any further advanced after toiling for so many years and continually depriving themselves?
The time has come to clear up a situation which can no longer be tolerated.
I appreciate that we were not sufficiently aware of the situation, just as I know that it was not through ill will that we have put up with such a monstrosity, as the granting of $10 a month for the welfare of the wives and children of our fellow citizens who work year in and year out in prosperous plants, offices, schools, universities and elsewhere for the progress of our country. 1 know that the pleasure and joy caused by progress in other fields of the national economy have taken the attention away from a still more important factor, that of the human being in his normal environment, his family.
I am quite aware of the fact that the success of companies and institutions is both useful and necessary. Indeed, we have
Supply-Health and Welfare dedicated the last 20 wonderful years, that is since 1944, to them but it is high time that we turn our attention with the same enthusiasm and with the same measure of success to the needs of human beings in our regular and honest families which are always a tribute to life, love and fecundity. Are life, love and fecundity to be encouraged, tolerated or criticized-in our capitalistic yet Christian society? Within the family, must life, love and fecundity be considered as economically important as they are in the production of goods and in the field of material and physical achievements?
So, there is an enormous gap between the purchasing power of the father of a family and that of a bachelor or of a childless married couple. Fifteen million people must get by with an approximate total income of $14,700 million while the other 3,500,000 have an equivalent amount to spend.
As taxes are in a large measure hidden in the purchase price of goods, the taxpayer who is obliged to spend all his salary to support himself, his wife and children, pays his income tax and also the taxes included in the items purchased out of his salary, so that he spends each year 100 per cent of his income on vital expenditures and taxes.
On the other hand, unmarried or married people without children can save and put aside part of their income on which they do not pay taxes at the time of purchase. There lies the fundamental unfairness, unfairness which is not compensated either by tax exemptions or small family allowances which are not high enough and which are not granted to all dependants.
That is what must be especially recognized in the unfairness of burdens people have to bear.
The man who has more children to support has less revenues to put a roof over their heads, to feed them and to pay for their clothes and education. The man who has more children has less money and pays more taxes towards society. That is what should be realized and admitted. That is where, in the final analysis, adjustments should be made. That is the solution we are offering here. And everybody would benefit, because an increased purchasing power, according to the number of children, would promote everywhere a better distribution of goods, production and professional services, and would help business, industry, agriculture and the whole economic activity of the small and medium firms. The large firms themselves would benefit by this increased economic

Supply-Health and Welfare activity in every sphere of the national economy.
After having realized how little compensation tax exemptions and family allowances represent on the income of the family heads, in comparison to the single people, when they earn an average salary of $80 a week, or $4,200 a year, what should we think now of wage earners who earn less than $80 a week; many wage earners earn only $40 a week, or $2,000 a year?
How about the small wage earner who does not earn enough to have his name appear on the roll of income taxpayers?
How about the people who earn less than $1,000 a year, for themselves and their wives, less than $550 a year for their children aged 16 years or over, and less than $300 a year for their children under 16 years old?
Do you think that these are just a few unfortunate people who should be ignored when we consider the population as a whole? There again, we fail to envisage reality if we do not pay attention to this.
Whether or not this surprises you, there are two million taxpayers whose names do not appear on the list of income taxpayers, out of seven million citizens who compose our labour force. Five million only appear on the list of personal income taxpayers, as there are about 80,000 companies appearing on the list of profit-earning corporations.
You may consult your Canada Year Book 1963-64, page 991-and you will have an idea of the distribution of income between Canadian citizens taking part in production and the income derived from their work or their capital. You can take from it the following details which put the situation in a nutshell:
First, 20 per cent, that is, 1.5 million persons, earn $6,000 or more a year, or $120 a week; second, 50 per cent, that is, 3.5 million persons, earn from $1,000 to $6,000 a year, or from $20 to $120 a week; third, nearly 30 per cent, that is, two million Canadians, earn less than the income tax exemption which would apply to them and their families.
Those are statistics given by the government in Ottawa. Now, am I the only one to come to those conclusions? Professor O. J. Firestone, a well-known figure in administrative circles in Ottawa, a member of the royal commission on health services, a professor and vice dean of social sciences at the University of Ottawa, made the following statement during the masterful speech he just
[Mr. Latulippe.l

made in Manitoba before business and labour leaders:
Canadians pay a great deal of attention to the 300,000 unemployed, while ignoring almost entirely the 3,800,000 Canadians who live in poverty, whether they are unemployed or not.
And this, even though Canada ranks second in the world for the highest per capita income and alternates with Sweden between second and third place for the highest standard of living.
Those 3,800,000 Canadians, one out of five, 20 per cent of the population, have an income lower than the minimum necessary to buy the necessaries of life.
This statement adds nothing new to the reality of economic imbalance, of the iniquitous distribution of income and burdens of society in our prosperous and progressive Canada. This statement adds nothing new, but confirms once again an unfortunate situation which must be corrected as soon as possible.
That statement was made by a university authority acknowledged and appreciated by our Ottawa authorities, by our political leaders, since Mr. O. J. Firestone was a member of the royal commission on health services in Canada, whose report was submitted to the governor general in council in Ottawa in April 1964.
Do those statistics and reports not suggest that we do not live any better in Canada than in underdeveloped countries? Not any better than in South Africa? Not any better than in India, where there are 300 people per square mile, against six people per square mile here in Canada?
I feel it is high time to put an end to this unbearable situation which most members of this house deplore, even if the 26 powerful ministers go on ignoring it and pretending not to admit the real facts.
What did Mr. Mackenzie King, prime minister of Canada, say in 1944, during the debates in the House of Commons which preceded the passing of the Family Allowances Act? Our ministers might still in 1964 hear the words of that former Liberal prime minister, who can reproach them for having misunderstood his lesson and the spirit of the legislation sponsored on that occasion. Here is this statement which has been considered so important that it is reported in a work published by the International Labour Review, Vol. LXXV, No. 3, March 1957:
Out of the citizens forming the labour force, 48 per cent are bachelors, 39 per cent of those who are married or widowers have no children under 16, and 40 per cent of those who have children under 16 have only one child.

It must be specified that 84 per cent of children under 16 are dependants of a fraction of only 19 per cent of the labour force.
To train the next generation is the responsibility of less than one fifth of the labour force and it is only fair that the expenses incurred be supported by all.
There might be an excuse if the general condition of the national economy required such a strict and faulty distribution of production and wealth. But no, this country of ours, Canada, is considered as the second nation in the world. But no, the following statistics will make it clear that if some people lack the necessaries of life, others enjoy prosperity and the security which it gives, while piling up surpluses, profits and capital that can be envied by the most ambitious capitalists in Canada and even in the world.
Here is, for instance, a few samples of the general prosperity in Canada with regard to great factors of the national economy and their constant progress between 1944 and 1964. Let us take the year 1944 because it coincides with a general survey of finance and banking that year and with the establishment of family allowances which have remained at the 1944 level while all other sectors increased three, four, five, six, eight or nine times.
Let us have a good look in order to see where and how the Canadian economy may be improved.
The principal ministers are responsible for this situation.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has control over all the administration of the country and its citizens.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) has to keep watch mainly on economic justice, which concerns all citizens in the most sensitive material and physical areas: money, cash, the vital minimum purchasing power.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) controls all the monetary, economic and political machinery and procedures for levying taxes on incomes and profits. It is incumbent on him, especially, and on others also, to analyse the incomes, expenses and profits among citizens, families and institutions.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) keeps an eye on all the relations between the population and the ministers, and above all, he is an economist and understands professionally the significance of the primary financial needs, of the vital strict minimum for each citizen, as an individual, in the family circle and in the framework of the private and public institutions.
Supply-Health and Welfare
The Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) knows very well that the whole of the production is intended for consumption and not for warehouses or capitalization. He knows also that the total purchasing power distributed among labour and among capital following production, directly affects only
7,000,000 citizens in Canada and leaves without income the 12,200,000 dependant citizens: children, students or adults unable to earn a living on account of age, illness or unemployment.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) knows quite well that trade is going at a slow pace, because there is unemployment and even poverty, even among families where the head is working at a single man's salary. Equal work, equal pay.
Every line of business would be more prosperous and more efficient if each citizen were to receive as a matter of right a minimum living allowance, over and above his wages as head of family which he receives in return for his labour.
Those six ministers must examine this proposal and consider that it is a problem for which they are personally responsible. All 26 ministers would readily approve any decision thus taken. The Minister of National Health and Welfare would only have to distribute $30 instead of $6 and $8.
I understand that to bring up family allowances to the level of the cost of living in all economy sectors, they should be raised to $30 monthly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would ask you to impose order on a rather exuberant member here.
I might say that not only were these questions directed to co-ordination by way of a federal department of aging, but provincial governments have been active in this field, as well as welfare agencies. Hundreds of senior citizens across the country have formed clubs and groups in the different provinces to organize recreational activities for older people. From experience in my own riding I would say that churches of various denominations have also done what they can for older citizens. I might mention that the Canadian welfare council is organizing a national conference on aging which is to be held in 1966.
While all of these efforts are most commendable and deserving of the highest praise, has this whole problem, I ask you, Mr. Chairman, been viewed in a proper perspective? Co-ordination of effort seems to be a desirable objective but it cannot be achieved until all parties concerned know what are the problems of the older persons as individuals-and I repeat individuals-and not as a group. There are hundreds and hundreds of reports, I am sure, in the minister's filing cabinets and in cabinets across the country, all of them dealing with some segment of the problems of the older citizens, but they are all written from the group standpoint.
We know, for instance, that it is almost impossible for a person who is 65 years of age or over to get employment. We also know that there are many reports prepared on the prospects of employment for older persons, but who knows how many of these persons need employment? Therefore, I am saying that specific information is needed rather than the generalities which have so far been compiled. This information must be available in Canada, either through governments or agencies, before we can make progressive headway with a solution to this problem. Such information would be invaluable if it were available, not only to the minister's department but to other agencies of government, and certainly for the purpose of the forthcoming national conference on aging; and it is essential if we are to achieve any concrete results.
Now, what are the problems of these older citizens? It is easy to provide or to suggest an all-inclusive or blanket answer, but I submit this would be inadequate because of
Supply-Health and Welfare the numbers, variety and complexity of our older people. If I can refer to the transcript of the Senate committee on aging, the Nuffield survey of old age conducted in Britain stated the position simply as this at page 59 of the report, that "all old people do not like the same things". In our studies in this country so far we have not been able to find factual material assembled on a national basis which collates and evaluates these problems. Therefore I submit that the only way to find out and to get a truly national picture is to ask the older people themselves, and it is for this reason that I suggest to the minister and to this committee that she inaugurate a national survey of the needs of the older people.
Now, Mr. Chairman, what am I proposing? I am proposing a nation-wide survey of Canadians who are 65 years of age and over. Why am I proposing this survey? I am proposing this so that the minister can find out what the problems are concerning these men and women in this age group. What are some of the problems? Financial insecurity and housing are two. If I might refer to the transcript again of the Senate committee on aging, it is reported at page 59 that:
A study of housing for older people which, is now in progress under Canadian welfare council auspices may be available in a few months, so I shall not deal further with low rental, self-contained accommodation which may be built, but I must emphasize the importance of suitable location.
Other problems are easy to find, and I am sure hon. members have had them brought to their attention in their capacity as members of parliament. There is for example the cost of illness, cost of drugs, cost of hospitalization, the need to augment income, inability to get employment. Despite the fact that he or she has arrived at the age of 60 or 65 years, a man or woman is still able and willing to work and deserves work. The reduced purchasing power of pensions is another problem. Then there is the domestic problem which arises after retirement. Any wife in such circumstances can testify to the difference in the domestic scene when a man who has been working for 40 or 45 years is suddenly compelled to spend most of his time at home. In addition, because there is a surplus of leisure time there is often an addiction to alcohol.
From what I have been able to learn during my brief experience in my constituency, it is suggested there is a difficulty among older women in readjustment when the retired husband spends all or most of his time at

Supply-Health and Welfare home. There is an interference and dislocation of established normal habits in the home. There is, resentment toward the restriction of personal freedom enjoyed before the husband retired. There is difficulty experienced in respect of the cost of accommodation and the inability to obtain employment. There are many problems affecting widows particularly, including the financial, hospitalization and the cost of drugs.
Mr. Chairman, you might ask me, as well might the minister and her advisers who look at me with some interest and perhaps some scepticism, what would be the value of such a survey? It would reveal on a national instead of a local or regional basis, what are the major and common problems among Canadians 65 years old and over. I submit with great sincerity to the minister that such a survey would result in the assembly of valuable and accurate statistical information. Such information could be the foundation on which the federal government could formulate a policy to deal with these problems. Has such a survey been made on a national basis, Mr. Chairman? To the best of my knowledge no such survey has been made.
I should like to quote from the evidence of Mrs. Jean Good, who appeared before the Senate committee on aging. At page 67 of that evidence, in answer to Senator Grosart, who asked the same question I have posed now, she said:
I really do not know. This, as you mentioned, sir, requires investigation in Canada. We do not know enough about the cost of living.
Then Senator Roebuck said:
What we should really be doing is searching around for what we can do or what we can recommend to be done, including an increase in the pension and everything else that might help the lot of the older citizen.
Then Senator Grosart again says:
I think we should get at the facts.
Mr. Chairman, how would a survey be conducted? It could be conducted of course by co-ordinating other government agencies, and it might well be done under private auspices. I can anticipate the arguments of the advisers to the minister who are sitting before her. I know they would say at the moment that there is a committee in the other place in respect of aging; but the honourable senators who have sat on that committee, and the witnesses who have appeared before it, stated that the main problem was in assessing the needs of the aging. Assessing the needs of our so-called older citizens is difficult because of the lack of concrete information and

facts. Of course the minister's advisers may well say, we are holding a national conference on aging in 1966, and that will take care of the problem. Surely this national convention will not prove to be of much value, or of as much value as it could have, unless it is able to operate on the basis of concrete information assembled between now and that time. I would therefore in this brief intervention urge the minister and her advisers, in cooperation perhaps with the Department of Labour, to institute on a national basis a survey of the older people of this country, to ascertain from their own mouths what their problems and needs are, and not impose upon them suggestions preconceived by experts, and preconceived by professions which deal, admittedly in a dedicated way, with their problems. We should ascertain in this way from their own mouths the hopes, frustrations and expectations of these citizens.
I am sure the minister has had this quotation of that great prime minister of Great Britain, Mr. Disraeli, drawn to her attention. He said, let us hope that the heritage of old age is not despair. This problem will become more and more direct, and it will be incumbent upon the minister as she proceeds with her duties to solve it. I urge her to give consideration to the suggestions I have made this evening.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak for a short time in respect of this item because I was a member of the committee which Hon. Waldo Monteith chaired.
Mr. Chairman, I think I am as good an example of health as anyone in the house, taking my age into consideration. I know some of the officials who are sitting before the minister at this moment and would like to make special reference to the lady who several years ago was private secretary to the then minister of defence Hon. T. L. Ralston.
At that time I had the privilege of being one of the junior members of this house and that was, as you will remember, during wartime. I went to Colonel Ralston's office in an attempt to get a boy released from the army. He was a married man, but because he was married after the deadline he was considered by the army to be single, and was drafted. This man had 250 acres of land and stock to look after. There was no one on his farm except his wife and his aged father to do the chores, and this was in February, during the winter. His wife and father asked me to try to get him released from the army so that he could look after his farm. I asked them whether this boy had asked for a postponement of his draft and they informed me that he had not, on the basis of information supplied by a neighbour to the effect that he would not be drafted because he was married. In any event he was drafted into the army and his father was attempting to do the chores on his own farm and on his son's farm.
As I suggested, I approached Colonel Ralston's office and found that he was not in Ottawa. I might say that Colonel Ralston was one of the finest members of parliament I have ever met. Colonel Ralston's secretary, the lady presently sitting before the Minister 20220-497
Supply-Health and Welfare of National Health and Welfare, informed me that she could not get this young man out of the army, and that he was to be moved from Camp Borden to Red Deer, Alberta. I told her that he might just as well be released now before being moved to Red Deer, because I intended to get him out of the army and there would be the extra cost involved of bringing him back. She said: "What will I do"? I said, "Call the official and try to get him out". She did. They did not believe me. They sent an official down to the farm to see if I was telling the truth, and I was. He was given six months leave and was never back in the army again. That was an example of a good secretary.
I had a letter today from two elderly people between 65 and 70 years of age asking me if there was any chance of the government lowering the age to 65. They do not have much means of support and are not able to work. They were wondering if the age limit could be lowered to 65 and asked me to do all I could to have that done. They also asked whether the pension could not be raised from $75 to $100 a month because they said they have to pay rent and have very little means. I am passing this on the minister without making any comment whether it should or should not be done.
In the first instance however the old age pension was never intended to keep people alive but rather as assistance to them. In this day and age people seem to spend their money as they make it, and when they grow old and are not able to work they fall back on the mercy of the government. I do not know what we are going to do about this situation because it involves circumstances over which we have no control.
I want to speak for a moment about the Canada pension plan. As hon. members know, a Canada pension plan is to be brought forward. We have been trying for some time to have it introduced into the house but up to now we have not been very successful. The other day I was reminiscing in my office and I composed a little poem. I am sure the minister will not object to my reading it because it contains nothing detrimental to her.
Judy tried as best she could
With a pension plan she understood.
But when Pearson and Gordon got through with her script
Poor Judy's plan started to slip.
They mauled it around from pillar to post
'Til there's nothing left but a ghastly ghost.
They're on their fourth translated test
And it seems to me even worse than the rest.
The only hope I see for success
Is let the opposition bring in a test.

Supply-Health and Welfare
They've been a wonderful help in the past
And there isn't a doubt their plan would last.
I am only trying to help the minister. I always like to help ministers because I find that when I am in the opposition it is much better to try to get along with the ministers than to quarrel with them, and you get more satisfaction that way. Having nothing more to say I will be glad to sit down if there is another speaker to take up the time of the house from now until 10.30.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I was referring, of course, to the health of the Liberal party. I should like to congratulate the minister and all members of her staff. I congratulate the minister because I think she did a much better job in presenting her estimates today than she did in presenting her first version of the Canada pension plan. I suppose this only goes to show that one matures in office and that the minister and others on the front benches across the way perhaps realize now that they have no divine right to rule and that probably a bit of diplomacy is better than the tactics they followed in the past.
I should also like to congratulate the minister on the fact that she will be occupying new quarters shortly. I suppose we might refer to her as the penthouse queen because I understand she will be occupying the penthouse in this wonderful new building with a view of both Ontario and Quebec. Added to the fact that she already drives a Thunder-bird, this is certainly a sign of affluence.
I do not want to say very much about the many items in these estimates. I associate myself with previous speakers who have spoken on specific subjects such as mental retardation, the aged, and physical fitness
[Mr. Cardiff.1
and sports. I am sure both the minister and I should lend our support to the physical fitness program because we are good examples of poor physical fitness. I should like to congratulate my confrere, the hon. member for Kamloops, on his speech regarding research grants in medicine.
I should like to say a word about the food and drugs committee of which I have been a member. I think the committee is doing valuable work and in my view Dr. Morrell and his staff are doing a wonderful job under somewhat trying circumstances. I hope the minister will pay heed to the recommendations which the committee will make with regard to increasing his staff and having to do with the conditions under which they work. As a personal observation I would say that although the food and drug directorate is doing a very good job, it seems to me their efforts are not as widespread as they might be and are not reaching those who could have a direct effect on the economics of prescription drugs. I refer to the individual doctor, dentist, veterinarian or druggist. To this end I have suggested in the committee that some improvements in the labelling and grading of drugs be made and I hope these suggestions will be reflected in the committee's report and that the minister will take some action on them.
I was one of those who supported youth allowances. I understand that some parents are under the impression that the cheques will be sent directly to the children. I would ask the minister to make clear to the house exactly what the mechanics of the administration of youth allowances will be and whether the amounts payable will become part of the family allowance cheques or whether separate cheques will be sent to the young people individually. It seems to me that if these cheques are sent to the young people individually the administration of the allowances will cost a great deal more, and I certainly see no reason why they should be handled in this way.
I should also like to congratulate the northern health services officials. In the northern part of my riding we have a number of health clinics which provide health services to the Indians and the local people. We also have two new hospitals in my riding. One is the fine new hospital at the new Whiteshell atomic energy research centre in Manitoba and the other is the new wing of the hospital at Pine Falls, built at a cost of half a million dollars. It is interesting that in this new wing Indian health services are being integrated with the general hospital

facilities in the community. I am proud to say that the people in the Pine Falls community have accepted this integration and perhaps this is a good portent for success in the future.
I want to congratulate the minister on her stand against smoking. As a member of the dental profession who has to clean people's teeth I want to wish her every success in this campaign against smoking. I might mention that at the recent convention of the Canadian dental association the minister's stand against smoking was endorsed and, as I say, we wish her every success in this undertaking.
My main purpose in speaking tonight, and I make no apology for it, is to bring to the attention of the house and the government some factors relating to dentistry as they apply to the federal government and the people of Canada. I make no apology for this because I did not hear anything in the minister's introductory remark about this subject, nor have I heard any of the various speakers mention the subject in discussing these estimates. I think the importance of dentistry to the community at large might be better appreciated if people realized that approximately 33 per cent of the amount of money spent on health services in Canada is spent on dental services. The latest figures which
1	have are for the year 1962 and they indicate that Canadians spent for these services some $395.2 million, and for dental services $132.4 million. This is a very significant sum of money. I mention it, Mr. Chairman, only because I want to relate this sum of money which, as I say, amounts to something like 33 per cent of the amount spent for health care services by the Canadian people to the amount of money allocated by the department to dental health programs and dental research.
I should like to say that only about 1 or
2	per cent of the amount of money allocated by the federal government under national health grants allocated to dental research. It seems to me that this is a negligible amount. In fact, in the last three years this amount has been decreasing. The percentage of money allocated for dental research as related to the expenditures on all health research in 1961-62 amounted to 1.79 per cent; in 1962-63, 1.42 per cent; 196364, 1.14 per cent. In the last three years, therefore, it can be seen there has been a steady decline in the relative amount of money that has been allocated by the federal government to dental research. The amount in dollars and cents was, in 1961-62, $67,911;
20220-497i
Supply-Health and Welfare 1962-63, $50,312; 1963-64, $48,009. We might compare this with the amount that was allocated in 1959-60 which was $164,264.
I note that the Canadian Dental Association has made representations to the minister in this matter, and I hope that before we leave the first item the minister will give us some indication of the action her department has taken toward alleviating the scarcity of funds for dental research. As I say, the Canadian dental association has made representations and I am sure the minister will realize it is urgent that this amount of money be increased. I should like to refer to the brief presented to the royal commission on health services by the Canadian dental association. In the introductory portion of the brief the association asserts, with regard to dental disease, that the unnecessary tragedy of dental diseases is one of Canada's greatest health problems. Dental diseases are largely preventive, yet they are virtually universal. Almost everyone needs dental care yet in any given year only one third of the population visits a dentist. At another point the brief states that, by their very nature, dental diseases defy defeat without widespread application of preventive medicine.
This brings me now to the fact that we need to spend a great deal more money on research in developing further preventive measures because we are dealing with a disease which is largely preventable. I am reminded of my second pet subject, that is fluoridation. Fluoridation, as a public health measure, is probably the least expensive that is practised in this country. I think it costs around 12 cents per year per person to fluoridate the water in any fair sized community. This is indeed a very small amount of money when we consider the amount of money I have already mentioned as being spent on dental health services in the country. This is one dental health preventive measure which I think should commend itself to the government. It is a field in which I feel the government should take leadership. As I said, dental diseases are largely preventable. Statistics have shown that among the children of dentists, dental caries are some 40 per cent to 50 per cent less than in the population as a whole. This I believe is attributable to better health knowledge and education. I feel that before the government rushes into medicare or rushes into the socialization of dentistry and medicine, they should assume responsibility in the fields where responsibility lies on their shoulders, that is in the field of dental education and medical education as well as the prevention field.

Supply-Health and Welfare
I feel that the federal government has been very remiss in this field. I believe that there is a great responsibility which they have failed to discharge. Before I conclude my remarks tomorrow I will show the government that it is incumbent upon them to assume a larger responsibility in this field.
